Mr. Chairman, since coming into this house I have noticed that when one makes his initial contribution, if it can be considered a contribution, to the proceedings, the usual procedure is first to eulogize the riding from which he comes.' This is a special session of the house, however, and I am going to forgo that pleasure, except to say that the people of Wellington North sincerely believe that they live in the banner constituency of the finest province in the greatest country of the world; and I heartily agree with them.
I desire to give some reasons why I am in favour of this resolution. I do so as an Ontario farmer. I want to make it clear at the outset that I do not pretend to speak for agriculture as it concerns the whole of Canada; I do not know enough about it for that. Having lived all my life within five miles of the farm on. which I am now living, however; and having spent about nine years on the local county council, meeting farmers from all parts of Ontario as they gathered to discuss county matters, if I ever hope to appreciate some of the problems affecting Ontario agriculture I believe I should be able to do so now.
It has been suggested by several hon. members that this legislation should be broadened in such a way that it would more directly affect the people of this country. I have been unable to find out whether or not those who are suggesting the need of further controls mean that they should take effect at once or at some future time. I have been unable to find out whether they wish an over-all freeze, or just a partial freeze. I noticed that this morning the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar neatly sidestepped a question by an hon. member on this side of the house, as to whether or not he was in favour of the immediate freezing of wages. As I say, I am not too clear on that point; but my understanding of the controls advocated, beyond those provided in this legislation, would be

an over-all freeze of wages and prices right now, and from that point of view I should like to offer a few suggestions.
We were called here primarily to deal with the national crisis resulting from the railway strike, and the government brought in for our consideration Bill No. 1. Before coming here I had the privilege of meeting a group of railway men who live in my riding, and had the benefit of their views as to why they believed they were entitled to higher wages and shorter hours. The legislation brought in by the government has been fairly acceptable to these men. They are not transient labourers; they are solid citizens, home owners and all the rest of it. They considered they had a legitimate cause; the Prime Minister stated that they were acting quite within the law, and I was glad to hear the Minister of Labour endorse that statement in Toronto on Labour day. Having in mind the fact that this dispute has not been settled, if we were to impose a wage freeze at the present time, as has been suggested, it would be extremely unfair to these men; so I suggest that is one angle we should consider.
Then from time to time we hear complaints about the cost of living and the cost of food. As a farmer I should like to mention a few things that I believe have been lost sight of for a long time by the consuming public. In the first place I believe that for many years the consuming public have been accustomed to cheap food. Probably the people who are buying it will not agree with that statement; still I maintain that for many years the people of this country have enjoyed food which has been sold at less than the cost of production. If we farmers had figured our costs as any other industry does he would have been away in the hole. From time to time we have been accused of being income tax dodgers, and we always reply that we do not know where we are at; that we are not very good bookkeepers, and I think that is true of most farmers. Now, however, we are starting to figure our costs a little more closely, and as a result of that figuring I do not believe there has been any increase in the production of food in this province. In other words we are beginning to realize that for a long time we have been selling for less than the cost of production.
One of the features of that cost of production which has been given practically no consideration by any person is the part played on the average Ontario mixed farm by the housewife. Before I left home we were fortunate enough to finish our threshing, so I had my grain in before I came away; but when we were working at that job we started at seven o'clock in the morning and quit at
Essential Materials (Defence) Act half past eight at night. That necessarily meant that the chores in the morning, afternoon and evening had to be done by someone else, and in most cases it was the housewife who did them. If you asked any of those farmers whether he was making any money on his hogs, first he would figure how much he had to pay for feed; then he would add another $4 or $5 for bis own work and another $10 or $12 for the price of the weanling pig; but I venture to say he would never give a thought to the hours of work put in by his wife. We farmers are very unfair to our wives in that regard, and I believe that is something which should be taken into consideration, especially in this day and age when we hear so much about wages and hours of work.
Many people are asking for shorter hours and more take-home pay; and let me say right here I am not opposed to that. I am a firm believer in the philosophy of wages we heard enunciated so often by the late Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, who time and again said that he was in favour of the highest wages the traffic would bear. I want to go on record as subscribing wholeheartedly to that theory. 1 have no quarrel with any who ask for a forty-hour week with forty-eight hours' take-home pay; if they think that is feasible and that the industry can carry that burden, it is all right by me, and I for one would not oppose them. But, sir, to my mind this is the $64 question. So far as the cost of what we consume is concerned, I wonder if these people ever stop to think what the cost of production of foodstuffs would be if the farmers of Ontario suddenly decided to work forty hours a week. I have in mind the hours of work that are put in by the average farm housewife outside of her ordinary household duties. I think I am safe in saying that they work at least four hours a day outside their ordinary household duties. The average Ontario farmer still works at least ten or perhaps twelve hours,-I quite readily agree that conditions have changed in the last few years owing to the advent of hydro in rural communities throughout Ontario, and I am quite willing to admit that farmers do not work as long hours as they used to work.
And they get no overtime pay.

We do not consider overtime. Let us say that the farmer works ten hours a day, and add to it the four hours a day the housewife contributes; that makes fourteen hours a day. You do not need to be an Einstein to calculate it. The majority of the farmers in my riding, if they adopted the forty-hour week, would have their week's

Essential Materials (Defence) Act work done, considered from the point of view of hours, by Wednesday night. I have no quarrel whatever with the fellows who can secure the forty-hour week if their industry can stand the pressure. But I think people should be fair. I think the people who have achieved those wage standards and hours of work should realize that they cannot expect the price of foodstuffs to go down.
We have heard a lot of beefing about beef, Mr. Chairman, since this session began. Apparently some people are worrying about the price of beef today. I know that when my wife goes to the butcher shop to buy beef a couple of dollars do not seem to go very far. There is a lot behind the present cost of beef. Over a period of some years I think I am safe in saying that I have had livestock on the Toronto market for at least forty of the fifty-two weeks in the year. Sometimes I have not had very much, but occasionally when my banker calls me in at the end of the week I realize that I have been there too late with too much. I am quite sure that the present cost of beef can be attributed to a condition of scarcity. What is the cause of that scarcity?
I believe there are several causes for it, and not the least is the fact that for a number of years the beef producers of this country were faced with an embargo under which they were not allowed entry into world markets in which beef would bring more money than it did in Canada. I believe the farmers agreed to that because they felt it was their patriotic duty to do so. While there was the occasional protest, in the main the farmers of this country readily agreed to produce at what they knew was less than cost. I know my friends the wheat farmers will say that the same was true of wheat, but I do not know anything about that. I am dealing with conditions in Ontario, about which I know something. As a result of that there was not any increase in the number of cattle the farmers kept.
We have to bear in mind also that in Canada today we have over two million more mouths to feed than we had at that time. We have to bear in mind that the country to the south of us has a population of millions more than it had before the war. Since this government granted us access to the United States markets, we have been getting good prices for our cattle. Probably the cattle have been liquidated faster than is good for the country. The whole thing boils down to a dollars and cents basis. Today a farmer can realize $300 on a heifer that under ordinary conditions would be kept at home and used for breeding purposes. 'The farmers are not breeding them; they are

shipping them. Day after day I have seen loads of Holstein heifers and beef type heifers, that would ordinarily have been kept at home, going across the scales to be killed. This means that our cattle production is not increasing.
I point this out to those who say that the price of beef is too high today. So far as I can see there are two or three things that can happen. Either we shall have to pay more for beef, or we shall have to eat less of it, or both. I do not think it would be fair to pick out one particular section of agriculture and say that product is too high in price, while leaving the remainder of the products alone. I am in favour of price control if it goes right across the board. Unless it goes right across the board, I am not in favour of a greater degree of control than is provided for in this resolution.
I would say, sir, that I can see no immediate prospect of a drop in the price of foodstuffs that are produced on the Ontario farms. Do not forget that we have to meet urban wage conditions. If I am going to hire a man I have to provide him with facilities, and I have to provide him with hours of labour somewhat approximating those he can get in the large urban centres. Otherwise I do not get him. I am not kicking about wages. Any experience I have had in hiring men for the farm or perhaps for driving a truck has taught me that if you pay a man well he will give you a good day's work, but if you try to cut down his wages he will not. I am in favour of fair wages; but I do ask people to be fair about things and give the Ontario farmer a break. I believe there are other members here who could tell of similar conditions in their province.
I mentioned that one had to consider the cost of production. In this connection one could make a comparison between the cost of pop and the cost of liquid milk. Today milk is selling for about twenty cents per quart. In the newspapers I have seen some protests that that is too much, but if we consider the cost of production we will find it should be thirty cents a quart or the same price as pop. I am not saying for one minute that we should not drink pop, or that it does not contain some food value, or that some members of the house are not directly interested in it. I just cite this instance to prove my point, that if the farmer based his price on the cost of production, the same as the manufacturer does, the price of milk would be more than the price of pop.
I would say that at the present time I am in favour of this resolution, and the bill that is proposed. I do not think it would be fair to Ontario agriculture to have the price

of agricultural products frozen at their present level. I heard some person mention the fact that an embargo should be placed on the shipment of beef to other countries. I would say that no government should prevent us from taking advantage of that United States market which is so accessible to us; no government could justify an embargo of that kind unless it was prepared to substitute some form of subsidy to compensate the farmer for the loss of an export market.
May I add that I believe a subsidy to the producers is to all intents and purposes a subsidy to the consumer. It means that that particular commodity is retailed at a lower price. If the government should, however, be faced at some time in the immediate future with a crisis that necessitates the freezing of prices, I think I can assure them that, so far as the Ontario farmers are concerned, this is one branch of industry in this country from which they will secure every co-operation.

Inasmuch as what we have already heard is not quite right, I think that the correction should be made in this chamber.
The form letter to which the hon. member referred yesterday is one which is used by the Steel Company of Canada to terminate the employment of drifters-that is, employees who just fail to show up for work, who do not clear their unemployment insurance books in the usual manner, whose whereabouts no one knows, and so on. In the course of time the Steel Company of Canada sends out this form letter to notify them that their services with the company are ended, their seniority rights cancelled, and so on. At no time was it ever intended that this letter should fall into the hands of any employee who had enlisted for the Korean force. Any employee who advised the company that it was his intention to enlist, or that his reason for failure to report for work was his enlistment, would never have received this letter. Employees of the Steel Company of Canada
Essential Materials (Defence) Act who so advised the company were told at the time they terminated their employment that the company policy with regard to reinstatement was not yet fixed, and that as soon as this matter had been considered and a fixed policy arrived at, they would be advised. In no case was the employment of that employee terminated, nor were his seniority rights cancelled.
I feel that the matter should be known, and that this information should receive the same publicity as did the hon member's remarks of yesterday.
With regard to this particular letter, as a matter of fact if an employee reports to the company stating the reasons for his failure to report for work-reasons beyond his control, illness, or any other such thing-he will be reinstated; and that is the policy which the company has followed in the past. If a worker simply left his job, with no intimation to anyone as to his intention, and, as sometimes happens, his fellow workers reported to those in charge that he had left, I do not doubt that this letter could have gone to him. Yes, Mr. Chairman, I am one of the first to welcome that correction; but I must say this. Accompanying the letter that was sent to me was another letter from the officers of the union which informed me that the matter had been taken up with the company and that the company had replied that this was the procedure being followed, and that they could not adopt any other procedure until the federal government had legislated protection for the employee who had enlisted. That was the gist of the accompanying letter that I received from the secretary of the union.

That, Mr. Chairman, is utterly at variance with the information I have. I wish to quote from a Canadian Press dispatch which reads in part as follows:
When it was learned that the man had enlisted, he received another letter saying, "As yet we do not know what policy might be formulated regarding any of the men enlisting in the armed forces. We have kept a list of all the names of the boys who have enlisted and when a policy is formulated we will know what the outcome will be."

That is exactly what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said.

I rise to protest, Mr. Chairman. If their policy is not yet formulated, how can they state it? I have assurance from the management of the company that there is no intention now or at any time to take seniority rights from these men who are in the service of their country. I am sure there are many other members of the House of Commons who know the reputation of this company, and I resent the implication which is being made in this particular matter.

I had not intended, Mr. Chairman, to take part in this discussion, but I happen to know something about the subject matter under discussion. The lady member is much in earnest in defending the reputation of the national steel company-
No, the Steel Company of Canada.

The Steel Company of Canada, I should say; and in believing that their word is good. In a matter of this kind, however, and knowing this company as well as I know it, I am not taking their word for anything.
Action is required by the federal government in the matter of the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act before the man going into the services has any protection whatsoever. Last night I had two of the top officials of the automobile workers' union-they happened to be in Ottawa on this particular subject-meet with government officials with regard to changing the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act in order that members of their union who enlisted might have some protection; not only do they want an amendment but they want it made retroactive to June 1 of this year. Those enlisting from the automobile industry have gone in with that sword hanging over their heads. There was no assurance whatsoever with regard to them. I suggest that some statement should be made, either by the Minister of Labour or by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, because they are both involved. I think the Reinstatement


in Civil Employment Act was administered by the Department of Labour, but the Minister of Veterans Affairs definitely has a responsibility also. In order to clear up that point-because it is bothering many of the boys who have gone into the forces, or would go in-there should be some assurance from the government that that act will be amended so that they may be protected.
As I am on my feet, I might as well say something about the proposal before the house. I should like to have waited until the bill was brought down and to have had a look at it; but the subject matter is not hard to discuss. The minister should have no difficulty in giving the answers to any questions that may arise under this legislation, because he has gone through it all before. That is why I am going to take advantage of this opportunity rather than to wait for the bill. There are two or three things that I have in mind which arise out of the minister's speech. I want to provoke his thoughts so that if the bill is not adequate now he will amend it before he brings it in, to avoid further discussion.
The first thought that I should like to leave with the minister is this. While the resolution itself recommends nothing specific, it states that the minister has the right to protect the economy of this country; to take whatever steps he considers necessary to build up the defences of the country for any purpose that the situation may warrant. It gives him the power to hire assistants, to fix their remuneration, and all of that kind of thing.
Our experience in the last war was that the minister did all that. He hired assistants, and he brought in dollar-a-year men who were made controllers. But the point I have in mind is that the industrialists of the country were completely protected in that mechanism by reason of the fact that they had men on the inside in control and controlling the commodity that their own organization was producing; in fact they had a direct representative in there making the laws that suited the corporation. He was paid a dollar a year by the government, but he was paid a lot of other things besides. He got a fairly good expense account, and so forth, but he was also paid his salary by his own company. In the first analysis he was working for his own company; he was controlling for his own company, and he was seeing that his own company's interests were protected. The point at issue is this: he was working for the country, but he was in control of the commodity that his company produced. In the allocation of materials he was in a position to allocate them to his own organization. It may be necessary to do that again, and the

If the minister finds it necessary to organize in the same way as he did in the last war,
I suggest that this time he should also bring in representatives of the people who actually produce. I would not suggest that the minister call them in and give them permanent appointments. Particularly in a time of war they have a terrific problem to handle. They have upsets in all directions. If you are to get production, that department has to run fairly smoothly.
In this legislation the Minister of Trade and Commerce is given the responsibility of reorganizing the economy of this country, putting it to work and fitting it to the needs to the extent that he thinks the situation requires. If he follows the pattern set in the last war, under this legislation he will call in representatives of industry and find out their requirements. He will ask for their co-operation. He has already indicated to the house that he gets that co-operation a hundred per cent. He is amazed, he says, how co-operative industry is. That is fine. You indicated to them in the last war that you can work with them. This time it would be much easier to get the job done; but the minister has not tried to get the co-operation of those on the other side of the tracks. He has never taken in the worker and through his representatives said: We are going to turn the economy of this country around; you are part of the mechanism; you have well-developed, fairly sensibly led unions, and we are going to ask for your co-operation; we want you to come in and help us in swinging the economy around.
Without actually making them controllers as such, my suggestion the other day was that the minister should set up industrial councils in the basic industries, such as steel, coal, packing houses, and so forth. All it means is that you call in one or two representatives of the union who, with the employer, sit down with the Department of Labour, and through their contact inside will be able to go back to their respective unions and report exactly what has been done, why it is being done, and why it is necessary. As I have seen it in the past, and as it is today-because fairly recently I talked on this subject to responsible people who are heads of unions-that has not been done.
Essential Materials (Defence) Act
I want to say this also. Having in mind the fact that the enemy we are fighting this time has already infiltrated this country-he has his agents and his cells built in that stratum of society, because that is where he can do you the most damage-something along that line should be done. The minister and the industrialists may be great organizers. He may get the best machine production in the country that it is possible to get, but if someone is in charge of those who produce with that machine and is able to pull the pin on you when he likes and thereby leave you without full production, you are in a pretty sad spot.
Having in mind the fact that these cells are there and these agents are very vocal, the responsible people in the unions who have, to fight that kind of thing are merely out on the sideline as spectators. They cannot get up and talk to their people with any authority, or with the respect they would command if they were placed in such a position that they know what is being done on the inside, and are partners in what is being done. If you give them that status they can go back and speak with authority, and will thereby be in a position to influence to a much greater extent the people for whom they work. I just leave that thought with the minister. If he is obliged to use the powers given him in this legislation at this time I would ask him to make those who produce a partner in the machinery that he is developing for production services. I think that is absolutely necessary.
There is another observation I should like to make. It has to do with the development of new plant, if it is necessary, or the conversion of industry for wartime purposes. The facts and the records speak for themselves. Industry was completely concentrated in the two central provinces. I said it was not good in peacetime, and it is definitely not the thing to do in the kind of war that we might expect. It is not the thing to have your war production concentrated in some central spot where it might be knocked out overnight.
The minister pointed out that the national income was around $16 billion, with a potential of $17 billion this year. If you take a look at that potential production you will see that it is largely concentrated in the two central provinces. There is nothing in the east. There is lots of room for it there. If you are to produce bombs, shells, small arms, and guns, the logical and most economical place to produce them is the closest point to the raw material. If you are to fight a war in Europe, the shortest route to Europe for shipping supplies of that kind, or to the

Essential Materials (Defence) Act other member nations of the North Atlantic pact, is on the north Atlantic seaboard, and the shortest cut to there is from either Halifax or Sydney. On the island of Cape Breton particularly you have the coal, the steel and the transportation facilities right at your back door. The whole thing can be done there in the one spot. There is a huge surplus of labour in the maritime provinces that does not want to be shipped out. They would like to stay home. The government could kill two birds with one stone; it could properly decentralize production machinery, and at the same time give work to people who have not had it since the end of the war, as well as to hundreds who are coming from the schools and who have no place to go, except to go somewhere else. There is plenty of raw material and labour, and it is situated right at the back door to Europe, so it can be shipped to the other free nations of the North Atlantic pact.
The minister has the responsibility this time, and will have the benefit of the lessons he learned during the last war. We could be excused then for some of the mistakes we made, but we cannot be excused this time. I should think that war equipment and plants built this time will either stand ready for operation or be in actual operation for a long time. I should like to look at it as a permanent arrangement, because the international picture does not look good and is not going to -clear up quickly. I say this because there are some pretty sensible people in the maritime provinces who will -co-operate with the minister if they -are given the chance.
Another disturbing factor is inflationary prices. It is amazing what the propaganda machine can do when it is turned on, given the proper voltage and turned in the right direction. We left Ottawa in the latter part of June, when the situation in Korea was just developing. The first broadcast I heard after leaving Ottawa was that the people of Canada were hoarding sugar, hoarding this and hoarding that, with the result that prices were beginning to go up. That is a lot of nonsense, and I do not think any sensible member in the committee would believe it. How much stuff can the people of this country hoard?
A terrific amount.

The incomes of eighty per cent of the people of Canada are such that they are just living from week to week. They can get three meals a day, and they might be able to pay their rent, but they cannot afford to buy better clothing. What are they going to hoard? If there is any hoarding it is done in the upper brackets among those who wish

to fill their cellars-and I am not even suggesting they do it. That hoarding suggestion is merely a slogan that was coined to hide what was being done by people like Canada Packers, who stored several million pounds of butter not long ago until they got a price increase for it. Hoarding was merely a slogan to cover them while they created an artificial shortage and got a price.
At the same time as this hoarding cry was going up, and at the same time as prices were increasing, President Truman was broadcasting to the people of the United States, telling them not to be disturbed, and pleading with them not to raise prices. There is no shortage; there is more sugar in storage in the United States and Canada than there ever was in the history of either country, and the potential supply never was so great
Nevertheless that price cry went up. We know why. One or two people in this country control sugar; they pull the strings. They can cause shortages when they like. They can create artificial shortages and raise prices whenever they feel like it. I hope the minister is not falling for that nonsense about hoarding, because all the hoarding that could be done by the average person in this country affects the picture very little.
The minister does not want to put on price controls, and perhaps if I had to administer his department I would not want to, either. There is a good deal of work in connection with it, heavy responsibility, and one would have to stick to his office and do a job. Yet there is no need for me to tell anyone in this chamber about the benefits of controls during the last war. The Minister of Finance did that.
At the beginning of the second world war the then minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, stood in his place and told the House of Commons that price control was the worst device the world had ever known; but he had to get into it later on. Self-discipline did not work in the early days of the last war, with the result that the government had to impose controls. Then, in the latter part of the period of the war we heard the Minister of Finance telling hon. members who sit immediately to my right, and who were demanding, "Off with controls; back to free enterprise; up with prices; down with wages," and all that kind of thing, that controls were the greatest device ever invented by man, and that millions upon millions of dollars had been saved for the Canadian people. He had the facts and the figures to prove it.
If the government does not want to put on price controls, then the next best device is to hold down prices. They have got to be held down. As to the excess profits tax, I know

the minister would not fix any unreasonable figure as the measure of profit which could be received. Perhaps he could take a base around 1944 or 1945, and state that that would be a reasonable profit. My view would be that even the base at that period would be unreasonably high; however, he could pick that if he wished, and anything beyond that could be classified as excess profits. There would be no use in raising prices because the excess would be taken from them. There weuld be no incentive to increase prices if the extra amount had to be paid back in taxes.
I suggest to the minister seriously that most of the basic industries in this country feel that within the last year they reached a levelling off. We see an organization such as the automobile workers making a five-year contract. It is not an easy thing to tie the average workingman to a contract for a period of five years. In that contract there is an escalator clause making provision for changes in the cost of living, but they are not in a position to negotiate on the price increases. Then there are other unions that in good faith a few years ago bargained on a longterm basis for the purpose of stabilizing the whole economy. Mine workers did the same thing when they tied themselves up under a two-year contract, with no escalator clause. They cannot open that contract. They felt that they were safe in tying it up for two years; yet their wages had been eaten into by the increased cost of living.
There will be unrest in those industries; that is what I am trying to say. Right now basic steel is about to make a contract. I know they were figuring on signing a two-year contract, but with prices running away they are going to hesitate, because they will have no assurance that prices will remain stable.
This part-war part-peace economy cannot be stable unless some device is used whereby these people will be given some assurance that there will be stability in prices. I do not believe it is true to say that had we not taken off controls and relieved the pressure, the stresses and the strains, we would have had a bad time in the immediate post-war period. I do not think that is right. There was considerable pressure all right. We remember all the industries who wanted to make more money and to take advantage of the shortages in consumer goods. There was plenty of political pressure brought to bear then, and people were pulling the minister in all directions. I do not think anything would have happened to the economy of this country except that which was beneficial. My conception of our price control machinery and our subsidies was that we never needed
Essential Materials (Defence) Act them more than we have needed them from 1945 to the present time. The fact that the United States did put decontrol into effect rapidly affected us to some extent because of our close connection with them.
I want anyone to answer this question: How many points has the cost of living advanced in Great Britain since the end of the war? Yet they have maintained their controls. I know because I saw the figures a year ago. From 1945 until about the middle of last year their cost of living had risen by only one point; that is all. Ours has run away. In addition, mind you, wage increase after wage increase was given in that country. They held their prices down with subsidies. Certainly they did, and despite all the ballyhoo, propaganda and nonsense that you see about Great Britain in the North American press, the progress she has made since the end of the war, with the machinery she has evolved, is greater than that of any other country in the world. That is a fact. Do not forget that Great Britain came through a war and was devastated. Compare Great Britain today with France, Belgium and the other countries that faced a similar situation.
Great Britain is a country that must export about fifty per cent of what she produces in order to live. I am not saying these things for propaganda purposes at all, because I am a Canadian and I am going to live in this country. I want to see the best possible devices developed for the people of Canada, and I say there are many things we can learn from the type of experiment they are making in Great Britain. We are told that we cannot institute price control because it is going to do this, that and the other thing. Nevertheless the trend is in that direction, and the more study and attention we give to it the better.
You have to hold prices down somehow if . you expect to sign agreements with the organized workers of Canada. Prices must be held down. The hon. member on the other side of the house who made his maiden speech a few moments ago-and I compliment him on his initial effort-said a lot of things that we have been talking about in the house for the last ten years. He said that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar skirted the question of wage control. He did not. Older members of the house will know that for the last ten years we have put our formula on paper many times. We are not ducking the question of wage control. The fact of the matter is that wages are controlled now, and there should be a proper price control system imposed, to be coupled with a certain measure of wage control. They go together, and you cannot help it.

Essential Materials (Defence) Act Prices are controlled now for the farmers. Government agencies fix prices, make initial payments and subsidize the industry, whether it is fruit, wheat, or what have you. I do not think there is a farmer in Canada who would want to get away from that system. They at least know what they are doing. They know what price they are going to get for their crop. They have some idea about marketing, and there are responsible people on these boards doing that kind of job for them.
Consumers are also entitled to have the government provide some protection, because I do not believe in fighting with the boss to get ten cents on my wages and then telling John Smith, who heads Canada Packers, to add twenty cents to the cost of living, making me ten cents worse off than when I started. Some responsible person in the government must draw the line at the point where that kind of economic anarchy shall begin or end. I definitely believe that if you are not prepared to face price controls, if you do not want to hold down prices by way of subsidies, if you do not want to control the incentive for runaway profits by the introduction of some measure of excess profits taxation, you will have to enact legislation against profiteering.
The price of sugar has risen about 3-1 cents since the beginning of the Korean war. I think that is a straight steal. I do not think the earning position of any corporation in this country warrants it. I also think it is not patriotic. It certainly is not giving the government the support they should receive at a time like this. If you do not get such support voluntarily, then I think you will have to enact some kind of law against profiteering. I think we should read the report of the prices committee again to see the kind of thing they discovered. A company like Canada Packers admitted that they held butter in storage. They said: Yes; we forced the price up and made ourselves a couple of million dollars extra profit, but that is business, and there is no law against it. The only difference between them and A1 Capone is that there was a law against Capone, and he had a gun. He had to do it the hard way. I consider it theft just as what A1 Capone did. The only difference is that it was legal.

I know that the minister knows all these things as well as I do. I want to assure him that, so far as we are concerned we consider controls necessary. If he is prepared to institute that kind of legislation, if it is made necessary, then he will have our 
support, even if he does not have that of anyone else, in enforcing such controls and seeing that the right thing is done. I can assure him that we will help him in every way we can. The last time it was industry and the government. This time let it be industry, the government and the worker. Let such a mechanism be developed that we can remove suspicion, place the worker in the position where he too will have representation, where he too will plan the economy and will know exactly what is going on on the inside. Then he can go back and say to his people: I was there, I agree with that, I think it should be done, and this is the way it should be done. His people will have some respect for him because he has been elevated, has a status, is on the inside and knows what is going on. Then he can talk to that little pipsqueak with the line of chatter who represents Uncle Joe in this country.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has covered a good deal of territory. I always like to listen to his speeches, because he is a realist. I also try to be a realist. However, I should like to correct one or two impressions he has of the last war. We had controllers for industry, and some of them were dollar-a-year men, but they were not made responsible for their own industries. We did not follow that policy. We appointed a cement man to control steel, a glass manufacturer to control coal, and a banker to control oil. We did not select a man from the industry concerned to control that particular industry. During the war we did our best to bring labour into the orbit of government administration. My hon. friend will remember that we tried to develop labour-management councils in war plants, and with some success. I think a good many are continuing at the present time. We were not successful in getting councils in one hundred per cent of the plants. There had to be good labour relations in a plant before we would institute a labour-management council, and that was not found in all factories.
Then we had the labour councils meet with us in Ottawa to discuss the over-all policies. If we had to face the same situation again we would build on the experience of the last war, and I would hope do a better job in that regard. I think we realized then, just as we realize now, that we must have the co-operation of labour as well as management to do an efficient production job.
I do not know that I can cover the ground that was covered by my hon. friend with respect to price controls in the last war. Again I say he is a realist because he admits that we

cannot have price control unless we can also control the price paid to labour and workers generally. He and I saw price and wage control initiated in 1941, and we saw the whole thing blown sky-high by the steel strike of 1944. Price control was never fully effective after that time. The point I am making is the one that 1 mentioned before, namely, that to have effective control we must have the co-operation of every section of the Canadian people, and we can only hope to gain that cooperation under the stress of war conditions. We had no trouble at all in obtaining the co-operation of everyone in Canada during the period from November, 1941, until early in 1944. Pressures were building up; distortions were occurring; injustices were being perpetrated and perhaps accentuated. The situation was bound to blow up some time, and it was the steel strike that really ended effective price control in this country. My hon. friend says the United Kingdom has price control. It has; but it also has wage control. That country has had a freeze on wages; but reports indicate that it is facing a situation today in which the pressures are building up to a point where that system may break down. Price control is not a course to be undertaken lightly; and I sincerely believe that the legislation we have before us today represents the workable extent to which we can impose distribution and price control under present conditions.

A good deal has been said about price control; and the discussion today, I think, has shown parliament at its best. The discussion has been full and complete, an exchange of views in a manner that should be more typical of parliament than it is. The minister has discussed the mobilization of the nation; and if this resolution is in fact translated into legislation he will have all the powers necessary for that purpose. I now intend to ask him a question that is being asked today by a large segment of the population; it has to do with the wheat farmers of the prairies.
In connection with the British agreement there was in fact a fixation of prices and a maintenance of the wheat price at less than could have been secured on the world market. Within the last year and a half, as the minister knows, there has been a great deal of interest in what, if anything, will be. done with a view to making up for the lower prices farmers had to accept as a result of the control of wheat prices under the British agreement. That question is not asked only by farmers; it has been discussed at political party conventions, where resolutions have been passed, and I think some answer should
Essential Materials (Defence) Act be given at this time. People want to know what, if anything, will be done by way of compensating the western farmer for having been required over the years-and I am not entering into any controversial discussion now-to accept prices-for his wheat that are so much below world prices. Now, having regard to the fact that if we are to mobilize this nation, each group making up the nation must have the assurance of fair dealing, I ask him again what is the plan of the government for compensating the farmers by adding to that which is now to their credit in the pool. No one knows exactly what the amount now to the credit of the farmer is, but using ordinary powers of computation and deducting what one would expect to be the reasonable cost of operation of the board, there is nothing to indicate that the amount to be distributed would, be more than ten cents a bushel. Will any additional amount be paid, or is there any suggestion of it?

I have explained several times that the government would be in a position to consider the final payment from the pool as soon as the wheat has been sold and we can know what can be paid out. I find it difficult to understand the reference to compensation. My hon. friend is talking about the five most profitable years the farmers ever had in the peacetime history of Canada, so far as payment for wheat is concerned. I could tell him the British analysis of the situation, if he cared to hear it. Perhaps this is not the time or place for that, however; it might better be done when speaking to the farm organizations later on. Up to the present the government has never been accused of being unfair to the wheat growers of western Canada, and when the pool can be wound up I think my hon. friend will find that the government will deal with the situation in a way that will be fair to the farmers.

Is there any hope that
there may be some compensation?
Well, my hon. friend can hope for anything he likes.

As I indicated earlier, Mr. Chairman, I believe the detailed discussion of this subject can best take place when we actually have the bill before us. Nevertheless I should like to put forward certain features of this resolution which it seems to me should arouse the interest of hon. members and cause them to examine with a great deal of care the exact extent of the powers which will be conferred by the bill when it comes forward.

The situation with which we are confronted is this. At a time when we found ourselves getting rid of the carry-over of controls from the last war, we are called upon to consider not only rearmament and the provision of money for that rearmament, as well as the necessary manpower; we are also asked to confer certain over-all powers which are said to be necessary for the purpose of carrying out most effectively the industrial and other activities by which we may prepare ourselves for defence on a much larger scale.
It has been generally conceded that part of the very system to which we are opposed is the control of the economy of the country by the state. Quite apart from whether a particular form of control may be approved by some part of the community, the fact remains that there has been general agreement that it is not desirable to place the whole economy of the country in the hands of any government. There has been fairly general agreement that the best way to protect our system is to have it operate as a free system in which the word "freedom" applies to all human activities no matter what they may be, as long as they are within the law and are consistent with the best interests of our people. For that reason it does seem that we should examine with considerable care these legislative provisions which will once again bring under the wide powers of the government the daily lives of our people.
The thing that has impressed me in the explanation given today is the similarity of certain statements that have been made to other statements that have been made, in connection with both the over-all preparations for national defence and the provision of the money required for that defence program. Members of the government have raised some objection to the suggestion that there has been complacency on the part of the government in presenting its case to this house. That was heard on a number of occasions when we were dealing with the resolution which had to do with national defence. There has not yet been the same opportunity to discuss the financing of this program which was placed before us last night, but once again the suggestion of complacency has been made. Today we have placed before us a general statement regarding the necessity for assuring the effective channelling of resources and supplies, so that our industrial and other production may be most effective for the purpose of building our national strength to meet the threat in front of us. Once again, however, there is this same tendency to leave the impression in this house, and to convey the impression beyond this house, that while there is a 

serious situation there is no impending threat on a scale that calls for tough words and an appeal to the people of Canadian to recognize the tremendous dangers which confront them.
It is true the Minister of National Defence spoke of the threat of communism. Having done so he then conveys the impression that we are going to take our place in the collective defence of freedom by one active army brigade for the defence of Canada, and one special brigade for the United Nations. We are dealing in terms of less than 10,000 combatants while those who present the threat to us are dealing in terms of many millions of men fully trained and armed to the teeth. Again in the case of the budget that was presented to provide for this limited recognition of the threat, although provided for at great expense, we had this effort that we must accept described as a hill on the road to peace. What a gentle and easy term to describe the threat that is before us, the threat implicit in the words of the Prime Minister, who accepted a statement that the really critical period may well be within the next ten months.
Where at any point in the statement of the Minister of National Defence is there a recognition of the fact that our fate may be determined within ten months? Where in the statement of the Minister of Finance is there a recognition of this challenging thought? Where in the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is there any suggestion of a threat of the nature that has been exposed to us by the tragic events in Korea in these past few weeks? The Minister of Trade and Commerce has left no doubt that the powers which would be conveyed by the bill, which we have not yet seen, would be wide and sweeping powers. He has indicated his belief that those powers are necessary so that this country may perform the task to which it is committed. I think that with very few exceptions, if any, the hon. members of this house are prepared to support every appropriate piece of legislation which will strengthen the defence of this country, both from the military and from the economic point of view. But here again we have the suggestion that, great though the powers may be, there really is not the urgency which should lead us to regard those as something that will be exercised in carrying out this task. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, having admitted without reservation that the powers are wide, did point out that the government will be in a better position to make arrangements with manufacturers and others if it has this power in reserve.
I believe that the words the minister used were these, or if not that they accurately

interpret the words that he did use. A word from the government is more effective if behind it there is a power that can be applied. We will all agree that is so. What the minister is really saying when he uses those words is, give me a club and I will do the job. At a time, Mr. Chairman, when we are seeking to preserve a parliamentary democratic system I strongly urge the members of this house to bear that in mind when the bill comes before us. In conferring powers upon the government as a whole, or any member of the government, we do have some concern about the possibility of passing a law which is only intended to be used as a club, even if it is not intended to apply the club except as a threat. I hope that when this bill comes forward it will state how the authority is to be exercised and will to the greatest degree possible retain under the authority of parliament that responsibility which is part of the very essence of the democratic system we are seeking to preserve.
We have no intention of voting against this resolution. At the moment the resolution stands in general terms. But before passing from this resolution stage and while waiting for the bill itself I urge the government, no matter what may be the content of the bill now, to recognize that part of the process of preserving democratic freedom is to retain the authority and the responsibility of parliament itself.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. Howe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 5, respecting materials and services essential for the purposes of defence and national security.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The bill before us, Mr. Speaker, gives legislative expression to the intention of the resolution which has been before us for some days and which has led to an extensive discussion of our national defence problems. While the bill stands in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), it in fact presents to the house proposals which have been dealt with by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton).
On second reading we are dealing with the principle raised by the bill. The principle inherent in this bill is the raising of money for the rearmament program and for the extension of military services called for by the international crisis which has become more apparent within these past two months. My impression is that almost all hon. members are in full accord with the principle that we should support those measures which are called for by Canada's participation in the plans for collective security which have been supported by this parliament.
Hon. members, however, have an obligation to make sure by every means within their power that whatever finances are provided will be used most effectively for the preparation of those defence forces which are called for by the international situation today. I have no intention of enlarging upon the details which have been discussed so extensively already. I do want to point out, however, that we still are not in a position to say what our real state of preparation is at this moment, nor are we in a position to say that when we have approved of those great expenditures there will be any assurance that they will be devoted to the most effective purposes in preparing our defence forces.
Last June this house approved of the resolution adopted by the security council, that the members of the United Nations should take joint action to restrain aggression in


Korea, and carry out the principles of the United Nations charter. That therefore is not in issue. At the moment the type of force to be sent to Korea is not greatly in issue. We now recognize the simple fact that so far as land forces and air forces, or combat air forces, were concerned, we simply did not have them for service, either in Canada or elsewhere, at the time this situation arose. We therefore accept the fact that for the defence of Canada, and for any other commitments, we should be doing whatever is necessary to assure that with the greatest possible speed defence arrangements will be made so that we can defend Canada and assume the obligations which are set forth in the preamble to this bill.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has pointed out that on three occasions in the last session we urged the appointment of a committee on national defence. He put that forward as a reason we should not hear any more about it now. My own impression is that the condition in which we found ourselves this last summer is one which supports with the utmost emphasis the need for a committee of that kind. If such a committee had been appointed at the time when this proposal was made last June, to say nothing of whether or not it had been made on the several earlier occasions that it was put forward, hon. members would have known more about the real state of our defence. That is past. Nevertheless we cannot ignore that past until we have some assurance that we have taken appropriate steps to prevent the same thing happening again. There is only one way we cam, namely, to have a committee on national defence set up now so that it may examine the plans, either in open session or in secret session as decided by the committee, and obtain that information which will make it possible for that committee to report to the government, and to hon. members, as to the real state of defence forces. After all, the state of those defence forces is the obligation of parliament and not of the government alone.
If these statements that we are reading in the press and hearing over the radio do correctly interpret the world situation as it is today, then, we are simply not operating in terms of reality when we accept the proposition that during these critical months immediately ahead we are going to prepare only two brigades, one for special service and one for the defence of Canada, and that there is going to be the slow increase in the strength of the Royal Canadian Air Force which is given priority as the major branch of our defence preparation.

There is none of that sense of urgency which is conveyed to us by all that is happening today. Korea is occupying the mind of every one of us. We must remember, however, that Germany could become another Korea on a far vaster scale, with implications that go far beyond anything that is brought to us by the events in Korea.
There are other places where trouble could start, and it could start at any time. Our one hope is to show now, and with the utmost speed, that here and in the other free countries we are preparing with a speed and a determination which will convince the men in the Kremlin. Does any hon. member think that the men in the Kremlin are going to be greatly impressed by the news that some months from now we are going to have a special brigade available? In the face of their 175 fully mobilized divisions and their 350 divisions which could be in the field in a very short time, is one special brigade, with three or four thousand combatants, going to leave very much impression in their minds of the urgency, vigour and determination with which we are playing our collective part in the responsibility of saving freedom for ourselves and for others? That is the issue before us. We can go only as far as the government is prepared to go. We can however seek to impress upon the government that this is not their responsibility alone, that the responsibility for preserving freedom is that of every Canadian, and that every Canadian has a direct, very deep and very real concern about the adequacy of the steps being taken.
Other governments following the same constitutional practices we respect have adopted the same method for keeping members informed. The system of committees is not new. We employ it in regard to many departments of government, and I submit that, far from the Department of National Defence being one which should be excepted from that general practice, if there were not other departments the Department of National Defence is certainly one which should be assisted by the constant supervision and suggestions which would come from a committee of that kind.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has said on other occasions that when members of different parties join in a committee of that kind there is an obvious tendency to forget party differences and to work together for the purpose of making the committee as effective as it can be. I am certain that if such a committee, made up of members from both sides of the house, were appointed, members with military experience in the various branches of the armed services
Defence Appropriation Act of this country, we would find many if not all the reports and recommendations presented as unanimous reports and recommendations. Hon. members would know from those committee members who have a background of real experience in this field that the stated policies of the government were being carried out in the most effective way, and that the money to be spent would be spent to the best purpose.
Hon. members are anxious to see all these things done as rapidly as possible. They certainly will support the provision of the money required; but at the same time I submit that all members of the House of Commons should be seeking a practical way to obtain the greatest possible information about the most important subject we have before us.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose of bringing this matter under direct consideration by all members of the house, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That Bill No. 2 be not now read the second time but that it be resolved that while this house is ready at all times to provide for our national defence and to meet our obligations under the United Nations charter, the North Atlantic treaty or any other similar instrument for collective defence that may be entered into by Canada, it regrets the circumstances connected with the introduction and prosecution of this measure, namely, that the government has refused and still refuses to allow a special committee on national defence to be appointed by this house during this session of parliament so that the house will thereby be able to ascertain the needs and requirements for such national defence and for meeting our aforesaid obligations.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the house for very long, but I want to reiterate the position we have taken regarding the rearmament program. We are behind the effort of the government to provide for the defence of this country and to provide support for the nations allied with us through the United Nations in the endeavour to prevent aggression throughout the world. On numerous occasions in this house my colleagues and I have placed before parliament the view that under no circumstances should there be any profit to any individual out of the provision of the weapons and the munitions of war. That view, of course, has been very largely shared by many who do not support this party in the house.
I regret very much that after the last war steps were not taken by the government to retain the machinery of production for which the country had paid, and which would have enabled us to carry out the rearmament program largely on a nationalized basis. I realize that to come before the house at the present time and urge that the factories, industries and so on engaged in the production of those things usually regarded as munitions of war should be nationalized would delay the effort we all want to see carried out as quickly as possible. Consequently I am urging that in these large expenditures we are going to make in connection with rearmament we as a house should direct the government at least to nationalize the production and sale of what I might call the principal armaments and weapons of war.
We have gone some distance in that direction, I am glad to say. As the minister indicated, the bulk of our shells, bombs and so on are being manufactured in our own efficient Canadian Arsenals Limited, owned by the nation, from which, therefore, there is no private gain. Over the years I believe a strong determination has been growing up in the country that some time or other we should endeavour to take the profit out of war; and, as I say, I regret that when the last war ended and we had an opportunity to retain in our hands and under our own control sections of industry that were manufacturing arms and

munitions, we did not take advantage of that opportunity, in order that we might be able to do something that I believe many of us, and certainly all of us in this party, think is desirable. I well remember the lengthy and strong speeches made by many members of this house when the defence purchasing bill was under consideration here. Particularly I remember the speeches by the minister in charge of the bill, the late Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie, who on March 10, 1939, as reported at page 1767 of Hansard, said:
The government, If I may speak for them, believe in the principle of equality of sacrifice; that in wartime men should not be required to offer their lives and limbs while those who provide the weapons of destruction have even the possibility of reaping undue profits.	-
That sentiment was shared by many hon. members. Last session we endeavoured to put into the defence purchasing bill a provision limiting armament profits but which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) stated could not be wholly carried into effect. That may be so, but at least the principle might have been accepted, and we might have endeavoured to exercise a control which would have eliminated the criticism that must arise if we allow profits to be made out of the provision of materials and instruments of war. Today I am urging the house that we accept the principle that at least the production and sale of principal armaments and munitions should be brought under national control, and I use the word "nationalized" in that respect. I remember that at the same page of Hansard Mr. Mackenzie said this:
The government is determined that in peacetime, where private industry must be utilized, there shall be the strictest possible regulation of profits both in the interests of the taxpayers and in deference to public abhorrence of profits made from products which involve destruction of human lives and misery among nations.
I am not going to put on the record again all the quotations that were put on Hansard, particularly by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) during the last session when we discussed a similar proposal. The record is there, and those who wish to read what he quoted at that time can do so. I recall of course that he quoted extensively from articles that were written by the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), and especially from a series of articles entitled, "Merchants of Death". I remember that the previous leader of the opposition, Dr. Manion, upon the outbreak of war in 1939, after referring to a statement he had made before the house was called, made some interesting remarks along the same lines. Dr. Manion quoted from a statement he had issued to the press a day or two before we met, pledging
Defence Appropriation Act support of war against Hitler, and he said this, as recorded on page 16 of Hansard of September 8, 1939:
At the same time, in giving this co-operation, it must be the steadfast determination of all of us that there be no profiteering of any kind-no unfair advantage taken by anyone-no enrichment for some while others are offering their lives.
Then in commenting on that in the house he said this:
I repeat that I consider that principle perhaps the most important that the government can adopt in carrying out this co-operation. I believe that all Canadians desire that that be carried out, and they desire it ardently. They feel that anything made in the way of excess profits by anyone at a time like this is, in a sense, blood money. The idea of some growing rich on the suffering of their fellow-Cana-dians is repugnant to everyone. It must not be permitted; there should be an absolute and rigid control to prevent it.
We concur in that view. In the house we have argued for the limitation of profit, and for the reintroduction of excess profits taxes at this session. In the budget that came down last night that was not done. I do not propose to criticize the budget just now. One of my colleagues will do that when the occasion arises. I want to place before the house as strongly as I can the belief of a great many people in this country, that if we are going to prepare for our defence and if we are going to ask, as we must ask, many of our young men and-if the worst came to the worst, which God forbid-many of our young women once again to don the country's uniform and stand steadfastly against aggression, the profit must be taken out of war.
In order that I may put this squarely before the house I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright):
That Bill No. 2 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the production and sale of munitions and armaments should be nationalized.
I do not want to delay the house but I feel that, having expressed this view so frequently and as strongly as we have, I should place the idea before the house in the form of an amendment. Though the resolution suggests, as it must under the rules of the house, that the bill be not now read a second time, the word "now" is the governing word. If it is defeated then we can proceed immediately to the second reading of the bill, but I hope the amendment will be supported and carried by this house.

Mr. Speaker, I am entirely in sympathy with the expressions which have been used by the leader of the C.C.F. group in regard to profiteering in the defence requirements of this country. There is, however, one difficulty raised by the wording of
