Defence Appropriation Act the amendment which I should like to point out. The amendment calls for the nationalization of the production of munitions and armaments. As the hon. member for Kose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has correctly said, I have advocated for some considerable time the elimination of profit from the manufacture of weapons of war which have no other use than for military purposes.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is the intent of this amendment.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I recognize that is the intent, and for that reason I have said I agree with the purpose of the amendment. I have not changed any view that I have ever expressed in regard to the making of private profits, and particularly what may be described as profiteering, in the weapons which could have no competitive sale. After all, rifles, machine guns, artillery weapons, submarines and things of that kind have no purchasers but governments. Believing as I do in a free competitive system, I also believe that the thing which protects that system is the competition. When there is no purchaser but governments for things of this kind, I certainly do not think they should be the basis of profit.
I have had occasion to express my opinion at different times about that type of production, particularly in the international field. I recall that one of those companies, which was one of the worst offenders in that field, was a company that sold only to governments throughout the world. This particular company had no competition because it had the overriding patent. It sold with complete and impartial disinterest to its own government, to Germany, to Italy, to Japan and to every other country. I mention this simply as an example, and it was the Electric Boat Company, which now wholly owns what was a national plant in Montreal only a few years ago. I object strongly to that type of activity in this field. Holding these views just as strongly as I do, however, and holding the very strong view that before we leave here we should have some assurance by legislation or otherwise that effective steps will be taken to prevent profiteering, particularly international racketeering in the things of war, nevertheless I regret that I cannot support an amendment which uses the words "munitions and armaments", because any clear definition of those words would embrace those other products which are today turned out by factories that are making other things as well and which, in my opinion, could not effectively be brought under a program of national production.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to make our position clear, I feel 

that I should say just a word on the amendment which has been placed before the house. We look with considerable sympathy upon the sentiments expressed by the leader of the C.C.F. party on the statement he made prior to moving the amendment. We have always felt that every effort should be made to take the profit out of war. Only by doing so will it be possible for us eventually to abolish war. There is no question about that at all. We should like to see every possible move made within our country to prevent armament factories or producers from making undue profits out of the manufacture of those things which are classed as munitions and armaments. We feel, however, that to nationalize the production and sale of them would not necessarily achieve the desirable aim that is envisioned in the amendment. I believe that we had in the last war enough experience in the manufacture and sale of armaments and munitions of war in this country to assure us that even when governments enter into the production of such things they are often obliged to call in private companies to operate the factories and that they cannot get the production unless there is some incentive to produce. At the same time, however, I believe that it is possible, without nationalization, to set limits on the profits that are to be made out of the manufacture and sale of armaments and munitions of war.
The thing that I believe we should give more attention to perhaps is to get at these fellows who manipulate the international exchanges and, through the manipulation of those exchanges, are able to manoeuvre countries into war. I am satisfied in my own mind that there is there a more prolific cause of international strife and rivalry than is to be found within the country in the manufacture of armaments. For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, although we are sympathetic to the intention, we cannot support the amendment.
Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North
Centre): I wish to say just a few words, Mr. Speaker, on this matter. I note that the last two speakers have indicated their sympathy with the aim of our amendment. Yet they have indicated, for the reasons they have stated, that they feel they must vote against it. I may say that it took a good many years of contending that the production of ammunition and bombs should be nationalized in order to achieve that objective. I was glad that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) was able to tell us yesterday that by far the larger part of the ammunition and bombs that we are manufacturing in this country is now being manufactured in our own arsenals. There was a day, no doubt, when sympathy was expressed with the aims

of those of us who sought that way of doing things with regard to ammunition and bombs. Accordingly, I feel that we must keep moving in that same direction with reference to other materials that go into the waging of war, particularly in the field of direct armaments such as guns, tanks, armoured vehicles and items of that kind.
The objection that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has made to our amendment is that some of these things to which I have just referred-for example, armoured vehicles and tanks-are made in factories which in peacetime make other kinds of vehicles or in wartime make both vehicles for use in war and vehicles for peaceful purposes. We recognize that difficulty, particularly now that we are right into the midst of a defence program. That is the reason for the emphasis placed in our motion on the production and sale of munitions and armaments. In this motion we dio not ask for the outright taking over of every factory that happens to produce within that factory, along with peacetime needs, some armaments and munitions as well. That is another question. Our contention, however, is that to the extent that a factory is engaged in the production of direct munitions and armaments, it should be nationalized and should be under the control of the government. Similarly, we contend that the sale of these articles to the government should be strictly under government control, so that profiteering in this line in which there is no competition, as the leader of the opposition has suggested, can be completely eliminated.
We welcome the expressions of sympathy that have been indicated for our point of view. But we feel that more than sympathy with that point of view is required at this stage in human history. As the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) has said, perhaps one of the ways in which to get rid of war altogether would be to take all the profits out of it. When are we going to do it? At the end of world war VI or world war VII? Some day when it is too late? I suggest that now is the time to take action in this matter, and I suggest that more than sympathy is required. I urge that this is the time for people who feel disposed in this way to indicate that they want further progress in the direction of taking the profits out of war by bringing the production and sale of direct munitions and armaments completely under public control.
Before I sit down, I should like to put on record one other paragraph from the September session of 1939. I was not a member of this house at the time but I well remember
Defence Appropriation Act sitting up here in the south gallery, as a visitor, and listening to the lengthy speech given on that occasion by the then prime minister, Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. As recorded at pages 22 and 23 of Hansard of that session, he said:
I come to profiteering. I believe I have already stated in this house that I know of nothing in the world more contemptible than that any man should seek to profit from the sacrifices which others are making. And if the laws and other measures which this government may introduce and seek to enforce are not sufficiently strong to destroy anything in the nature of profiteering, I hope hon. members of this house will bring to our attention, in a way that will also bring it to the attention of this country, what we ought to do to achieve that all-important end. There are some things that are very difficult of accomplishment. Unfortunately human nature has its weak and its bad sides as well as its strong and good sides. Sometimes it is very difficult to cope effectively with the underworld and its methods. But let me say this: I care not who the individual may be, how respectable in his own eyes or in the eyes of others he may appear, or what position he may hold; if in this crisis he seeks to profiteer, he belongs to the underworld and should be treated as one of those who menace all that is sacred in human relations.
That too is a strong statement of our point of view; and our point of view has received the sympathy of the last two speakers. I submit that if members feel as strongly as that about it, as strongly as we do, we should all do something about it as indicated in the terms of the amendment which has just been moved by the leader of this group.

As usual, Mr. Speaker, when the C.C.F. party start to talk about profiteering, they are being completely unrealistic; and to be fair with them,

Defence Appropriation Act I think they realize it too. Recently they had occasion to amend the Regina manifesto, after about seventeen years, and they have suddenly discovered that profits are something that are not too unrespectable. It took them seventeen years to arrive at that conclusion, and I would think that probably in another seventeen years they would amend their constitution to say that sex is here to stay, or something of that kind. They know very well that we need armaments in Canada; that the best way to get them at the cheapest possible price is to let some manufacturer have some incentive to produce them. I would suggest that the only standard of value the government can have is to have a real manufacturer with some ability, who will add up his books at the end of the year and say: I made a profit producing these things; I must have been reasonably efficient.
It is not a question of profiteering. The difference between profiteering and profits is one that is obvious to all of us. I would suggest that to tie in profits with profiteering, and make them sound as if they were illegitimate, is unfair. I would sincerely hope that whatever manufacturer takes over the production of war materials in Canada he will make a profit, because if he does I have great confidence that both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) will take most of it away from him and just leave him barely enough to keep him working hard.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) spoke of realism. There are two practical questions I would like him to answer. First, what would he do with the factories in peacetime? Second, would he succumb to political pressure by the workers in these factories and pay them between wars to sharpen up on their bomb-making along the lines of his suggestion that parliamentary stenographers should be paid between sessions to practise their shorthand?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Don't be ridiculous.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
do not know if the hon. member for Davenport's questions should be answered, for they are not germane to the question at issue. Does my hon. friend suggest that we must always keep factories that make munitions supplied with contracts, or that they must be kept operating when there is no war? I would suggest to him the situation is altogether different. We are asking young men- and we take only the best young men when they offer-to give their lives in war, whether it be police action such as we have at the present time, or whether it be a declared war against an enemy nation. If the men who do the fighting do not need the incentive of profit,


why must the people who in the safety of their places of business make the munitions and machines that the soldiers use have to be well lubricated with profitable returns?
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) says that we are not realistic when we talk about profits. Perhaps we are just as unrealistic when we talk about profits as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is when he talks about wages. I generally find that people are usually unrealistic about the things that do not definitely concern them, or when they feel they are being gypped out of something because someone else is being realistic.
At the beginning of this trouble in Korea I was really horrified with the-I do not know just exactly what word to use-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Any one will do.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
-the apparent satisfaction in certain sections of the country over the contracts that the United States by reason of the war was going to place in this country. Surely we are hard up for profitable business when we feel pleasure over business that comes to us in that way. Even if we are so hard up that we were glad to have war contracts we should have decency enough to cover up our pleasure.
Let us remember that it is abhorrent to the great mass of fathers and mothers of this country, whose sons do the fighting in this and every other war, that people should be making profits out of supplying them with the means of defending themselves and destroying others.
Apparently there is great difficulty in deciding what is a munition and an armament of war, because so many things go into war supplies that it is difficult to draw the line. But I am satisfied that there is a long list of materials that could be put in the category that this amendment would apply to. Until we have the will to do a thing there will always be difficulties in the way, but the moment that we have the will the difficulties will disintegrate into thin air.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
All through the pages of history I doubt whether there is any more despicable figure than that of the profiteer, whether it be the robber baron of ages gone by, whether it be the dishonest contractor during the period of the Crimean war, or whether it be the war lord in more recent struggles in Asia. Therefore I sympathize with the general idea behind this amendment that profiteering should be eliminated from the manufacture of all arms and equipment and that the manufacture of all munitions of war should be nationalized. Yet, I find it extremely difficult to know where to draw the line. Modern war embraces so

many different activities that I would find it extremely hard to say that this or that particular form of production is solely devoted to war.
I am thinking at the moment of the chemical industry. In my constituency there is an explosive plant which is manufacturing explosives for peacetime uses that during war converts its knowledge and know-how into producing explosives, partly for peaceful purposes and partly for munitions of war. One could go on from there to the forest industries, which are closely connected with our war effort, and all the industries connected with the supply of different types of vehicles, their spare parts and so forth, many of which are closely interwoven with the production of armaments, many of which must be maintained in peacetime in order to produce the requirements of peace, and yet will be able to turn over at very short notice to the production of armaments.
I deplore the idea of profits being made from the provision of armaments. The profit incentive no doubt is there. But even soldiers have other incentives during wartime. It was Shakespeare who said something about seeking the bubble reputation even in the cannon's mouth. And so I feel that for practical reasons I cannot support the present amendment.

Mr. Speaker, after hearing what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis) I thought it my duty to rise and tell of an experience I had during the last war.
A manufacturer asked me if I could get him an appointment with one of the officials in Ottawa connected with the supply of munitions, so that he might see if he could help the war effort. Through the office of the then minister of munitions and supply I secured the interview. We went to the supreme court building and saw a gentleman who, in turn, directed us to those in charge.
This manufacturer was interested in the production of dies. A die was shown to him, and he said, "Well, I believe this die could be made cheaper. How much are you paying for it?" If I recall correctly the amount stated was $14.37 each. He said that it could be made in a certain fashion and produced more cheaply, and stated that he could turn it out for a little more than $7. In a few weeks he got a contract at that price.
He began making the dies at the figure slightly more than $7, but after he got into production he was producing them for just a little over $4, and with practically no profit to his company whatever.

I believe that is what most manufacturers in Canada tried to do. I am referring of course to the established manufacturers, who tried to produce the best quality of goods at the cheapest possible price, so as to save taxes increasing, and to keep down the cost of munitions. In my view those manufacturers did a good job.
I do not feel however that the government should give contracts to those who are not established in business, or who have not manufactured munitions or other articles previously. I cannot vote for the amendment because I know what the manufacturers did in the last war and the preceding one.
I feel that if production were government controlled we would pay through the nose for the munitions we would get, and I am sure any established manufacturer could do the job better.

I do not want to be un-cooperative. I want to get finished and be out of here by the end of next week. I want to ask my hon. friend over here what we are going to do with this plant and equipment? When the last war started out national income was something like two and a half billion dollars. By the time the war finished our national income had risen to around $10 billion. The increased productivity in the country that boosted our national income arose largely from the creation of new industries established by the government for war purposes. At the end of the war the new war industries were converted to peacetime uses.
Our national income has now risen, as the minister indicated, to around $17 billion. The plant and equipment established during the war, and converted to peacetime uses after the war was over, have created an expanding economy, have boosted our national income, and are directly responsible for the condition that we have in Canada today. But it took a war and public investment to bring about that expansion. Canada is a young country. It is growing and there is plenty of room for expansion. I visualize that the time is not far distant when we will have fifty million people, and anything created by way of plant and equipment today can be used in the years ahead. It is not necessary to maintain it as a wartime set-up.
The training that our boys received in trades and so forth during the war was put to use. The only thing I want to see done at this time is that we start somewhere to take the profit out of war. We must define bombs, planes and that type of equipment and say that we do not want undue profiteering in their manufacture. When we are creating the new plant set-up let me say for the benefit of my hon. friend that we should scatter it across the country, decentralize it, and establish it in places where it can be used when the war is over as we used it after the last war.

Mr. Speaker, when resolutions of this kind are before the house we invariably hear a lot of talk that is very unrealistic in its nature. For instance, it is argued that no one should be allowed to profit as the result of war. I wonder if anyone really means that. When we recall the conditions in this country during the thirties, with the poverty that existed, and compare it with the prosperity that developed in the latter years of the war, and especially in the post-war years, when we realize that the prosperity we have enjoyed in the postwar years has been very largely the result of the war and of the unlimited markets created for our production, then is anyone going to argue that those who have prospered as a result of the war should not have been permitted to do so? Would a member of the armed forces be any better off if the civilian population were forced to remain in a state of poverty instead of being allowed to profit as a result of the war?
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) took exception to the manufacturers of armaments being allowed to profit on the arms and munitions the soldiers had to use, when those soldiers were sacrificing their lives for the country. Well, where are you going to draw the line? If the manufacturers of the guns the soldiers carry are not to be allowed to make a profit, why should the manufacturers of the uniforms the soldiers wear be allowed to make a profit? Why should the manufacturer of the boots the soldier wears be allowed to make a profit? Why should the manufacturer of hats, or the manufacturer of trucks be allowed to make a profit? And why should the producer of the food the soldier eats be allowed to make a profit? It seems to me impossible to draw a line when you start to argue in that way.
Some people believe that the manufacturers of armaments try to bring about wars in order to make profits; I have heard that argued in this house many times. I do not think that can be said as far as Canada is concerned. We know that here those who manufacture implements in peacetime convert their factories, largely at the request of the government, to manufacture arms. When they manufacture implements they make a profit. Why should certain manufacturers be asked to stop making farm implements and start to make arms without any profit, while the remainder of the industry continues to make peacetime goods at a profit? That seems to me a totally unrealistic attitude.
Defence Appropriation Act
Then we hear many people talk about the necessity of adopting the principle of equality of service and sacrifice. We all really subscribe to that principle, but we know it can never be applied. You cannot compare the service of a soldier in a theatre of war with the life led by a person in Canada. They just are not comparable. You cannot compare the filth, the mud and the torture suffered by the soldier with the kind of life led by a worker in Canada. Then how can you talk about equality of service and sacrifice? On the other hand, if we really desire to implement that principle to the greatest possible extent I think we would be justified in asking the workers in industry during a war to accept the same wages a soldier is paid and to work the same number of hours per week the soldier works when he is in a theatre of war. There is no eight-hour day or forty-hour week on active service. They are often fighting seven days a week, because no one takes notice of a Sunday in the middle of a battle. But then, would the soldiers be any better off if that principle were adopted? I have never heard of the soldiers asking that such a thing be done. I simply point out that the general principle of equality of service and sacrifice cannot be put into operation. It seems to me that if we want to back up our armed forces to the greatest possible extent we should ensure the greatest possible efficiency in the production of armaments. Can anyone argue that during the war, under government control and direction, private enterprise did not make a very good job of the production of armaments? I am not at all sure in my own mind that the nationalization of industry would bring about either greater efficiency or greater economy; I do not think history can show that it would.
If, as I take it, the intent of this amendment is to back up our armed forces, I would suggest the following things are necessary. First, we should adopt a truly pay-as-you-go policy, for unless we do so, what happens? A soldier fights overseas for perhaps four or five years; then he comes back and has to start paying for the war. I think the service of a soldier overseas should be recognized as his full contribution toward carrying on the war; yet when he comes back he has to pay taxes for the rest of his life to help pay the cost of the war he fought. Perhaps it is not possible to fight a war without debt, but I say it should be possible to at least exempt a soldier upon his return from that portion of taxation required to pay for the war. And then I would say that taxation during the war should be strictly on the basis of ability to pay in order to control profits at a fair level.

I believe that generally speaking we made a pretty good job of re-establishing our soldiers after the last war, though, mind you, there are still some things we should do.
So, in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that in my opinion the nationalization of industry will not help the soldier, and will not guarantee either efficiency of operation or economy in production.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in this debate, but I feel compelled to answer the statement we have heard from the very genial member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), and to my surprise from the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), that this group is unrealistic in presenting this amendment.
I want to be as brief as possible, but let me ask first, is it unrealistic to suggest that when one man offers his life in defence of his country, some other person or group of persons shall not take advantage of that situation to make excess profits, or to profiteer, as we call it? Is it unrealistic for those of us in this group to express what is without a doubt the opinion of many Canadians on this important question? The hon. member for Acadia belongs to the same veterans' organization that I belong to, and I have great respect for him, but I am sure he will remember that the Canadian Legion passed a very strong resolution urging that profit be taken out of war-in fact by passing a resolution urging the conscription of wealth and manpower for the effective and fair prosecution of the war. The whole intent of the resolution passed at that time was to eliminate profiteering as a result of war. Quite a number of churches in this country have passed resolutions supporting in principle the very amendment that this group is presenting to this house. Is it unrealistic to take notice of the opinions of large numbers of the church people in this country? I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that if it were possible and practicable to have a poll of the mothers of this country who have sons of military age, as to whether or not they would support this amendment, we would receive a large majority, fs that unrealistic, Mr. Speaker?
Of course, I know there are some groups opposed. I am quite sure the Canadian Manufacturers Association would be opposed. I am quite sure the Canadian Lumbermen's Association would be opposed. I remember in September, 1945, when this government was proposing to extend wartime housing because ~''H of veterans, the one organization

opposed to the entrance of the government into the housing field was the Canadian Lumbermen's Association. I presume they still have the same point of view with respect to the amendment presented by this group. We in this group realize the difficulties this type of resolution presents to a capitalist government, the difficulty of giving it full effect under a capitalist system. We present this to the house as a principle to be supported. It is a principle which is endorsed by large numbers of Canadians. I am not suggesting for a moment that we can nationalize all those industries that play a part in war production, because they are extensive and very widespread. I am suggesting, as did the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), that in order to show that this parliament believes in what is generally termed equality of sacrifice, it should be willing to endorse this as a principle and recommend to this government that wherever practicable under present conditions this resolution be given effect.
The member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) mentioned the prosperity that was brought to a large majority of Canadians as a result of the war. I think that is a sound argument in support of the deficiencies of this system. Unfortunately war, to most of the Canadian people except those who have lost relatives overseas and those who served overseas, has meant a period of relative prosperity. It is for that reason, when we are discussing this and other bills, that we hear members suggest or at least imply that there should be a war industry in their district. They are thinking of the fact that war and war preparations bring prosperity rather than the fact that war is a tragedy to this nation, and to the whole world. The member for Acadia mentioned the prosperity brought to the Canadian people as a whole. What it brought to the Canadian people as a whole, to the wage earners and salary earners, was a relatively decent standard of living. This resolution is not aimed at the great mass of people that experienced improved living standards; it is aimed at the monopolists who take advantage of their control of resources, processes and equipment to make exorbitant profits under war conditions. These are the people the resolution is aimed at.
I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, if we examined the balance sheets of the great majority of Canadian people and the balance sheets of the few corporations at whom this resolution is directed, we would see which of them had the reserves and which of them unfairly benefited from certain aspects of war production. In fairness, Mr. Speaker, I may

say that we recognize this government did an excellent job, on the whole, with respect to war production. We admit that, and I think it is generally admitted. It is most difficult under capitalism to have great war production without having profiteering creep in. I think it is only fair to say that in presenting this amendment to this bill we present it as a principle to this House of Commons, trusting that the members will support it as a principle, and in so doing indicate to the country that, when men are willing to volunteer to defend this country and our frequently termed Christian civilization, we are opposed to any profiteering at their expense, and that of the national interest.

Mr. Speaker, might I for a moment join the ranks of the idealists? In the discussion before the recess it seemed to be the tendency for those who were speaking on behalf of this amendment to be blaming the profiteers as such. I believe the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) made a good point when he said that patriotism was a sufficient motive to the young men who had to give up their lives in the field of battle, and it should be sufficient motivation for those who had to make the implements of war in defence of the country. As he knows and everybody knows, however, they demand their profits in addition. As a matter of fact they refused what I thought was a fair profit at the beginning of the last war in the matter of making munitions. I do not know that the individual profiteer is so much to blame. After all the system under which we live is motivated by profit. If it is legitimate to make a five per cent profit, if it is good business to make a five per cent profit, certainly I do not see why it is not better business to make a ten per cent profit. As a matter of fact there is no law of which I know against making profits.
There is a point which I did not think was sufficiently brought out in this debate, and that is that the very thought of war may became more acceptable, more palatable to people, because of the fact that during its operation these profits can be made. In other words it is a condition in which profits become possible. So far as I am concerned, I think war is an ill wind from which no good should blow to anyone. I have frequently heard the statement, as I am sure most hon. members have since the fighting in Korea started, "It is too bad, but one good thing about it is that business has certainly improved." May I repeat my colleague's words by saying that I too have the greatest respect for the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), but he did surprise me a little bit. I do not know 69262-31J
Defence Appropriation ACt whether he strayed from his usual common-sense approach; that is a matter of opinion. He has uttered one truth, and that is that the economic prosperity enjoyed by the people as a whole was as a result of the war. The deadly thing about that is that young people may begin to accept war as the lesser of two evils when they compare it with a state of depression. Acceptance of that idea might result in an unfortunate lessening of the resistance to war.
As to the charges of our being idealistic rather than realistic, I am not prepared as yet, in spite of the realism of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and others in this house, to give up my ideals. I wish some of the hon. members would tell me where idealism ends and realism starts. I might suggest, though I know I would be ridiculed for this particular type of statement in this very practical and realistic house, that idealism might even be considered as the true form of realism.

In that respect history is only repeating itself, because all down through the centuries that has been the process of democratic countries, namely that as soon as a war has been brought to a victorious conclusion the establishments for defence forces have been reduced until another crisis arises, at which time once again hasty steps are taken to build up adequate strength.

Had more vigour been put into the reorganization and maintenance of our armed forces following the last war, had more funds been made available during the past five years, then we would have had more troops ready to meet the situation which has arisen this summer. It cannot be denied that members on this side of the house have been advocating continuously the need for stronger defence forces. The next few months may well be a period of grave anxiety. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself has pointed out that it may be that during the next ten months a decision will be reached. During that period of time our defence forces will still be weak in strength. The result of the accelerated program cannot have been felt.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) pointed out that during the current year we can expect only two or three more aircraft. The new recruits which will come into the armed formations will not be trained men; they will have to undergo a period of training. The units, as personnel fill up their ranks, will have to undertake more advanced training before they are ready to fight as a team. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said, we are living on borrowed time.
I regret that fuller information has not been given, but the picture is sufficiently clear to indicate the needs that we have. I can only hope that the moneys which will be voted will be expended effectively and economically, bearing in mind that there are three phases in this problem. There is Korea, which is merely an incident in the present international situation. I express the hope that Korea will not be allowed to develop into what I would term a Spanish ulcer. During the Napoleonic campaign the operations in the Iberian peninsula drained the resources of the French army to the point where it was termed an ulcer. Actually, operations in the Far East might very easily develop along the same lines, and the resources of the democracies might be poured into that far-off country to an extent which would weaken our general position to meet what might happen in the future.
As has been said, the second phase perhaps will be that of other acts of aggression. And then there may be a third and final phase of general war. Those three phases must be borne in mind, and a balance maintained among those three in so far as the distribution of our funds and available resources is concerned. With those in mind, we all appreciate the necessity, so far as we are able, and without weakening too much our own strength, of providing assistance by way of resources and equipment to the other nations who see as we see.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 3, respecting the Canadian forces.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
Could we have a statement
by the minister?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
I gave a statement last
evening. It was brief, but I hope it was fair and adequate to explain the general purposes of this bill.

In the first place, it should be made clear that under the existing law of Canada, which dates back to 1868 and was re-incorporated in the National Defence Act adopted by parliament last session, it is provided that in an emergency the governor in council may place the forces of Canada on active service at home or abroad. That has only been done probably twice in the whole history of confederation. When we came to redraft the new National Defence Act we thought that hon. members would wish to have this provision preserved, and that was done in a substantial measure. The importance of it from the national point of view is that at any time when the active forces are put on active service at home and abroad, parliament has to be called within fifteen days, thereby preserving one of the fundamentals of our constitution, and that is the control of the people's representatives over the military forces. I could, if hon. members have not heard me enough in the last three or four days, give a good deal of historical background for that provision, background which runs all the way through British and Canadian history and is of the utmost importance. I shall not do that.
I shall start at 1868, and say that in the new bill we tried to preserve that principle, and I believe succeeded. We tried also to take account of the fact that fifteen days might be longer than was necessary to call a session of parliament, so the term was reduced to ten days. In the case of this session the members met, and met magnificently from every part of Canada and some parts of Europe, in less than ten days. It is believed, however, that ten days is a fair number, so that the act as it stands today requires parliament to be called within ten days of the governor in council placing any of the forces of Canada on active service. But the act also provides that that can only be done in an emergency. An emergency is defined by the act in section 2, paragraph 1, as meaning:
... war, invasion, riot or insurrection, real or apprehended.
When faced with the necessity of placing some of our active forces on active service outside the country under the United Nations charter, we were face to face with the necessity either of not regarding that as active service, as that term is defined, or regarding this as an "emergency" and that means war, invasion, riot or insurrection. Korea may be a really tough war, and certainly is for the people fighting it, but in the legal sense it is not a war but an act of aggression. We felt, therefore, some amendment was required to the act to take care of this situation. It was proposed that in addition to our being able to place the active forces or other forces of Canada on active service in an emergency.

as that was defined, we should also endeavour to obtain from this house the power to place them on active service, if considered desirable, in consequence of any action undertaken by Canada under the United Nations charter, the North Atlantic treaty, or any other similar instrument for collective defence that may be entered into by Canada.
As was stated last night, the function of our constitution is, and I think it is recognized now by all parties and certainly by this, that that sort of course would not be adopted without reference to parliament. The adoption of any instrument for collective defence that may be entered into by Canada applies to an instrument of international agreement signed by our representatives but only ratified by or after that instrument has been submitted to and approved by parliament. This course has been adopted by this government throughout, certainly in the case of the United Nations charter and the North Atlantic treaty which are most in point. The purpose of this provision is not, therefore, to extend the principle of the existing act but to extend the field in which the existing act may become operative so as to cover the present situation. That relates to sections 2 to 6 inclusive, which are consequential.
Section 7 of the bill provides:
The governor in council may by regulation provide that all or any of the enactments set out in the schedule shall, in such manner as the governor in council may prescribe, apply to
(a) any or all persons who, subsequent to the fifth day of July, nineteen hundred and fifty, were appointed, transferred or posted to, or enlisted, enrolled or serving in, any force designated by the governor in council as a special force for the purposes of this section;
The governor in council has already designated the force that we have raised, and which now totals by recruits, quite apart from any postings from the active force, as at five o'clock yesterday afternoon, 8,763, as a special force. Subsequently it is the intention of the government, if this bill passes, to designate other elements in the forces that may be actually engaged in Korea or may become engaged there, special forces so as to have the advantage of section 7. But that will have to be done, as hon. members know, with some caution because our idea is that we should extend to all the officers and men specially enlisted in the special force all the benefits that are applicable under the veterans charter. All of them are not, or may not be, dependent on the length of service, entitled to the benefits of the veterans charter as set out in the acts enumerated in this schedule.
The active force personnel-that is, the permanent force or the regulars as we know them -while on active service abroad with the
Canadian Forces Act
special force, will have the same treatment as they get but also would have, if they could qualify on return, the benefits that would be appropriate under the veterans *charter; Our anticipation is, however, that they, being permanent-force, full-time soldiers, would not qualify for many such benefits. To sort out the different classes and find out who is entitled to what, so as to do substantial justice and carry out the promise of the government that the men enlisting in the special force shall have treatment similar to that of veterans of the second world war, will not only require a good deal of working over, by officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs and of the Department of National Defence, but will also require the surveying of actual cases as they arise. It is the desire that, under this bill, we should have power by regulation to deal with immediate cases as they may arise-and we do not think there will be a great many-and to bring into effect such parts of the law as seem obviously to be applicable; and then at the next session of parliament to put before a newly-constituted committee on veterans affairs the question of determining what advice should be given to the house on how this arrangement should be worked out in detail.
There are a great number of different conditions, and it has been quite impossible for us, in the last three weeks, to draft legislation to put before this house as to how certain classes of veterans of active force personnel and of civilians enlisting in either the active or the special force should be treated. Therefore the only sound and proper course that would appear to us to be desirable is to ask hon. members to give us power to deal with the interim cases-and there will certainly be few of them-until this house meets again, and then to put the matter before a committee of parliament on which the various parties no doubt will be represented largely by veterans who have become expert in veterans affairs and which can hear, from the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Department of National Defence, veterans' organizations and anyone else who may desire to be heard, representations as to how any necessary changes in the law might be made.
Our general aim, however, is first to create one force. There is going to be no difference between the active force and the special force, except in term of enlistment and other matters consequent thereon. Our second aim is to ensure that as far as possible, and as far as seems proper to the members of parliament, the officers and men of the special force shall receive benefits similar in character, extent and application to those enjoyed by veterans under the veterans charter at the end of the
490

Canadian Forces Act
second world war. That will of course include -and the acts are mentioned in this schedule -the benefits of re-establishment in civilian occupation, a matter which was raised today by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis); and if the existing act on civil re-establishment does not cover the case he has mentioned, or even if it should, the place to discuss that matter first is, I suggest, either with the Department of Veterans Affairs or with the Department of National Defence, but ultimately with the committee on veterans affairs that we propose to set up to deal with just such matters.
I do not think there is anything else to be said about this matter. In consequence of this bill being passed, if it is passed, in both houses, we shall put components of the active forces of Canada on active service, and that action will lead to certain consequences which I mentioned last night. It will entitle them to the benefit of the insurance provision, provided they are a special force. It will entitle them to make a will in certain provinces in a special form. If they commit certain offences, it will make them liable to a special punishment. I do not know that it has any other consequences than those. There are some other consequences, but as hon. members can see, while they may be important they do not involve any great question of principle having regard to the legal consequences of the bill being made into law.
I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that this is a necessary move in the way of our doing our utmost to help the forces that are fighting on our side under the United Nations charter. I am sure that it is the first bit of legislation of this character, couched in such terms as actually to provide for action under the United Nations charter or under the North Atlantic treaty being considered as equivalent to an emergency. In that sense I believe we are making history and are cutting out a path that I hope some other nations may follow.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
In the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, it was forecast that legislation would be introduced to increase our national security and the international co-operation required by the fighting in Korea. It would seem that this is the legislation which will implement that forecast.
I think most hon. members came to this session believing that they were required to pass legislation authorizing the dispatch of the special brigade to Korea or elsewhere to fight under the United Nations' flag. This legislation extends the provisions whereby the governor in council may place on active service any service, component, unit or part of any of the armed forces of Canada not only for the defence of Canada in case of 
emergency but also to co-operate with the United Nations or to carry out commitments under the North Atlantic treaty or any other commitments which may be made. I think the essential point to note is that this proposed legislation gives the governor general in council authority to place troops on active service, to fight under the flag of the United Nations. But there is nothing in this bill, so far as I can see, that grants authority for the dispatch of this special brigade to Korea or any other place. If the decision is reached at some time or other to place this Korean force on active service in order to go to Korea or elsewhere it would seem to me that it will again be necessary for parliament to be assembled within ten days in order to grant that approval, unless there is some special legislation introduced during this session.
Today I was rather surprised to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) say that no other legislation was forecast, other than some administrative bill to deal with sessional indemnities. My impression of this-I may be wrong; if so, I hope I shall be corrected- is that while section 32 of the National Defence Act is now extended to make it possible for the governor general in council to place troops on active service, section 33 is in no way repealed or modified. Section 33 still requires parliament to be assembled within ten days after the placing of troops on active service.
Now, of course, troops of the Royal Canadian Navy, three destroyers, have been in Korean waters for considerably longer than ten days. These troops are not yet on active service. They are carrying out their police duties with the United Nations, still on what is termed) as being on service, a difference having been made in the National Defence Act between "service" and "active service", those units of the active or regular forces of Canada always being on service, but not on active service until they are placed on active service by the governor general in council and confirmed by parliament.
Therefore the first question that I would like to ask is whether it is the intention of the government to introduce definite legislation during this session, by which this special brigade will be placed on active service, to be sent either to Korea or elsewhere in order to co-operate with the other forces of the United Nations? It does not seem to me that Bill No. 3, as it stands now, gives adequate authority to the governor general in council to place on active service the forces which are now in Korea, and the special brigade which may be sent there in the future. That is the point which I hope will be cleared up. It is not clear to me at the present time. But

as I say, until section 33 of the National Defence Act is repealed-I do not think it would be wise to repeal it, and I do not think that parliament would agree to the repeal of that section-it seems to me that special legislation is required to grant the authority for placing this force on active service.
There is no very clear definition anywhere of what active service is. There are regulations which govern the troops when on active service, but neither in this particular bill nor in the National Defence Act is there any definition of what is meant by active service. As I said, there are regulations saying what must be done when troops are on active service but there is no definition of that.
Then I think the situation has been complicated by the introduction of this term "on service", which applies to the general condition of the troops of the active forces; but it also could be made applicable to troops of the reserve forces who may be placed on service, but only with the consent of the individuals themselves. However, I do not want to complicate the discussion by pursuing that any further.
The next point upon which I should like to make an observation is that dealing with the benefits which will be granted to the personnel of this special brigade. If the benefits of the various pieces of veterans legislation are extended to them, I think it is very regrettable that it has already been published in the press as press releases, and the statements which were made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) last night, namely that the personnel of this brigade would be granted the benefits of these various acts which are included in what is known as the veterans charter.
The bill says, and I am inclined to think rightly, because obviously further consideration must be given to it, that the provisions of these acts may be applied to the personnel of this special brigade by order in council. As the minister has already pointed out, I think that further consideration should be given to just which of those acts of veterans legislation should be made to apply. It is quite debatable whether a short-term force, a force which has been enlisted for only eighteen months, should receive the same benefits as men who were enlisted for what must appear now to have been a much more serious conflict than perhaps this particular Korean show is. Therefore, I think it is wise to give further consideration to how far the benefits of the veterans legislation should be extended to this special brigade. I repeat that I think it was unwise that premature publicity should have beeij given to the fact that 69262-32*

these men were to receive these benefits. We may be running into conditions which were perhaps not dissimilar to those which arose after world war II in so far as the fire fighters were concerned. They thought certain promises had been made to them, and later on they were disappointed when the promises which they thought had been extended to them were not being kept.
So I feel it is wise to give further consideration, and we should not decide prematurely that all these benefits are going to be extended to the personnel of the special force. Finally, I could not help smiling at the enthusiasm with which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) was prepared to appoint a committee to deal with a department other than his.

However, as the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) has pointed out, there are some aspects of the situation which are still not as clear as they should be made to us before this session ends.
The Minister of National Defence pointed out that the main purpose of the bill is to authorize the governor in council to raise a special establishment in view of any commitments we have made to the United Nations, or under the North Atlantic treaty, or by virtue of any similar commitments we might make. He also made it clear that its purpose is to authorize the governor in council to place those or any forces on active service in lieu of commitments we may have under the United Nations, the North Atlantic treaty or any similar collective security agreement.
With all of that we cannot but agree. That' follows from the support parliament has given to the government's support of the United Nations on behalf of Canada. In pass-' ing may I say that we agree, too, with the aim of the bill in so far as it seeks to extend; certain benefits now on the statute books to those who enlist with these forces. But the point that I think has not been made as crystal clear as it should have been is one touched upon by the hon. member for Nanaimo, and to which the minister referred, namely the bearing of section 33 of the National Defence Act on the present situation and, indeed, vice versa.
The hon. member for Nanaimo suggested that such-and-such could not be done unless, section 33 of the National Defence Act were repealed. I was glad to note his haste to add that section 33 must not be repealed. Likewise the Minister of National Defence has made

Canadian Forces Act
it clear that not only does section 33 stand on our statute books as something historic in our legislation, but that it has been slightly improved over the way it used to read, in that the term fifteen days has been reduced to ten days, referring to the period within which parliament must be called. speechtext:
I do not have any notes the minister might have had, nor do I know what he had in his mind, but it had been my intention to do just that. In view of what has been said I shall shorten what I have to say in this connection; but I do think that, despite our preoccupation with other matters, it is important for us to give attention to the processes of our parliamentary democracy. In view of this business of sitting all day, I have not had time to go all the way back to the year 1066, but I browsed around in the library at meal times today, and- I found that there has been on the statute books, certainly since 1904-I should say in parentheses that it may have been there longer-the provision now contained in section 33 of the National Defence Act.
When in 1904 parliament was writing that section into the then Militia Act, the question was asked as to where the wording came from, and the obvious answer was made that it was to be found in the Militia Act of the United Kingdom. In fact, Mr. R. L. Borden gave the answer-the question having been put to Sir Frederick Borden, minister of militia, who was putting the Militia Act through at that time-in which he stated that the clause then being put into the Militia Act of Canada was similar to section 19 of the Militia Act of 1882 of the parliament of 'treat Britain and Ireland.
That section 19 read as follows:
Whenever Her Majesty orders the militia to be embodied. if parliament be then separated by such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall be issued for the meeting of parliament within ten days-
This of course was in Great Britain.
-and parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such proclamation, and shall continue to sit and act in like manner as if it
had stood adjourned or prorogued to the same day.
Thus that language-substituting "on active service" for the word "embodied"-found its way into the Militia Act of Canada, which was 
passed in 1904, being chapter 23 of the statutes of that year. This was section 71 of that act:
Whenever the governor in council places the militia or any part thereof on active service, if parliament is then separated by such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall be issued for the meeting of parliament within fifteen days, and parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such proclamation, and shall continue to sit and act in like manner as if it had stood adjourned or prorogued to the same day.
When the statutes of Canada were revised in 1906, that same wording was carried forward in the Militia Act, which was chapter 41 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906. It remained as section 71, and the wording was exactly the same as that in the statutes of 1904, from which I have just read.
When the statutes were again revised in 1927 the same wording was again retained, so I need not repeat it. This year, however, the expression "militia" was deleted and other words were put in so as to correspond with modern practice. Thus we now have section 33 of the National Defence Act, which reads as follows:
Whenever the governor in council places the Canadian forces or any service component or unit thereof on active service, if parliament is then separated by such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall be issued for the meeting of parliament within ten days, and parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such proclamation, and shall continue to sit and act in like manner as if it had stood adjourned or prorogued to the same day.
That provision had indeed a long history and tradition behind it. This year, when the National Defence Act was rewritten and reenacted by parliament, the only change that was made is the one already referred to, namely, that the time within which parliament must meet has been reduced from fifteen to ten days.
One of the things that interested me in studying this matter, although probably I should have known it, was to find that this was required by law. I remember so well the speeches made by Mr. King, especially during the years just before world war II, to the effect that parliament would be called in the event of war, that parliament would decide whether or not the Canadian forces would be put on active service and sent overseas. I had the notion at the time that that was merely in the nature of a promise made by the prime minister of that day. I find now that his promise was clear-cut and categorical all right, but it was also based on the requirement of the law.
As hon. members will recall, in 1914 war broke out on August 4, and on consulting Hansard, as well as the Journals and other records of that day, I find that on August 4,

Canadian Forces Act
1914, the cabinet took the action oi placing certain of the forces then in Canada on active service, and on the same day issued a proclamation for parliament to meet on August 18. That was fourteen days later; in other words, within the fifteen-day requirement. Similarly in 1939 war broke out by the action of Germany against Poland, as we all remember, on September 1. On that day the forces of Canada were placed on active service, and the same meeting of the cabinet which passed the order in council placing the then forces of Canada on active service passed another order in council arranging for a proclamation for parliament to meet on the 7th of September.
I have in my hand the orders in council that Mr. King laid on the table the day that parliament met in September, 1939. There is quite a batch of them, but in particular it included those two orders in council of September 1. During the debate in the session of 1939 Mr. King referred to all these things that had happened, the fact that under an earlier section of the Militia Act the militia had been called up prior to September 1, 1939, but that it had not been put on active service until September 1, which was the day that cabinet at the same time took the decision required by law to summon parliament within what was then a fifteen-day period.
Similarly during the course of the debate Mr. Ian Mackenzie, who was then minister of defence, made the same point clear. The point was that prior to September 1 he, as minister of defence, had the power to call up the militia, but it was not until the cabinet had taken the decision as required by law to call parliament within a fifteen-day period that they could put the forces of Canada on active service. It seems to me this is not just a matter of tradition and history. It is not just a case of being interested in a technicality. It seems to me that this is very basic and fundamental to our whole concept of parliamentary democracy. As I have said on other occasions, parliament is a little bit closer to the people of Canada than the cabinet, by the nature of things, can be. The people of the country think of the 262 members of parliament, the backbenchers in the main, as their representatives. Somehow or other it is deep in the hearts of our people that major and important decisions should not be made by the cabinet alone but by parliament as a whole.
It is true that the requirement of the law that I have just indicated does not say that parliament has to approve of the action of the government in placing the forces on active service. All that the law seems to require is that parliament must be here and be sitting within fifteen days, now ten days, after the
proclamation placing the forces on active service has been made. Mr. King said in 1939 that parliament would make the decision as to whether or not Canada would go to war. He said that the government had made up its mind what its policy was and parliament would express its view by giving or withholding support from the government on that issue. I remember one very interesting exchange that took place when Dr. Manion pointed out to Mr. King that he had said something in one of his speeches that was not in the speech from the throne. Dr. Manion wanted to know if that was included in any vote of confidence in the government, and Mr. King said yes, that the house would make its decision by voting confidence or non-fidence in all that the government, through the Prime Minister, had declared to be its policy.
We are moving into a different kind of world. Things have improved in some ways but in other ways they have become much more critical and serious. I am wondering just how this is all going to work out in a world in which there may not be declarations of war such as there were in 1914 and 1939 but something different such as police action under the United Nations or under the North Atlantic treaty. As a matter of fact, we have had a pretty clear undertaking that no action will be taken under the North Atlantic treaty without the decision of parliament. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made that clear to us again the other day when he said that if there were any move, for example, against one of our partners in the North Atlantic treaty, the government would call parliament to make the decision as to what to do about that situation.
But where are we now with respect to the special force that we are raising? Where are we now with respect to any other outbreak of aggression that might perchance occur when we are not here? I hope it will not, but we have to face that possibility. As the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) points out, this session can end and members be sent home without our being told what the plan is with respect to the special force. I am hoping that what we are saying will draw forth a clear statement from the government because it would seem that if the special force has not yet been placed on active service then if the government decides to place it on active service after we are home the law says that parliament must be summoned within ten days.
The government may get around that by placing the force on active service before we go home. Let us suppose that is done. Then

Canadian Forces Act
what happens if there should be aggression somewhere other than Korea? I think the government should be particularly frank and straightforward with us in connection with these matters. You see, the requirement of the law does not state that the governor in council must place forces on active service for a particular place. We might assume that action taken by order in council was taken in respect of Korea, but a couple of months from now there may be a need somewhere else. Will the fact that the Canadian forces have been placed on active service for one area, while parliament is here, result in the possibility of these forces being sent somewhere else? In my view, that should not be done. As has been made very clear, our commitment in regard to Korea is under the United Nations. Commitments under the North Atlantic treaty are different in character. A couple of days ago the Secretary of State for External Affairs stated clearly that if we were required to make any commitment under the North Atlantic treaty parliament would be called. As I say, if the forces are on active service already the legal advisers of the Department of Justice might find it possible to say parliament need not be called, but I would deprecate such a course being pursued.
I believe the point should be made perfectly clear. I think the government should take us completely into their confidence and tell us what their plans are in connection with the force now being raised. I believe we should have the sort of clear-cut statements we have had in the past, and deservedly so, as to the intentions of the government in relation to parliament, as far as any future situation may be concerned.
I am not indulging in any criticism in this as far as the past history of Canada is concerned. The law was lived up to in 1914; parliament was called within fourteen days of the date the forces were put on active service. In 1939 parliament was called within six or seven days of the date the forces were put on active service. The present situation is different, but at least the government has called parliament. We may say they should have called us sooner, as I think they should, but at any rate we are here. The record is good thus far in the relation between government and parliament with respect to this matter of our forces going to war, whether it is declared war or police action, and I think it all important that this relationship be maintained between government and parliament and between parliament and the people.
As I have said, my own view is that section 33 is fundamental to our parliamentary democracy and the rights of our people. I am glad
the hon. member for Nanaimo hastened to say that it should not be rescinded or repealed or changed in any way. I also think it should be lived up to, not only in letter but in spirit. There should be no suggestion at any time of taking advantage of anything in order to get around the spirit of that section, which says clearly, as it has said from time immemorial, that putting our forces on active service makes absolutely necessary the calling together of parliament. In other words when it comes to going to war, whether it is war as declared between nations or whether it is a collective security police action, that is the kind of important decision that should be made by the people themselves through their representatives in parliament.
From what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has said tonight, and from what has been said previously by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and on other occasions by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), I feel they are with me in this, so I do not think I have to argue it. I did think it was possible, however, that the house might be so preoccupied with other matters this session as not to get this issue right into the open and have it made perfectly clear. I hope before we leave-it could be now, or later in this debate, or later in the session, but certainly soon-it will be made perfectly clear just how the matter stands as to the responsibility of the government to parliament, which is there all the time, but which is particularly clear and important in this matter of putting our forces on active service.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
I think the matter should be made perfectly clear at once, so there can be no misapprehension or uncomfortable feeling about it anywhere. When this bill is passed and becomes law it is the intention of the government to comply with the letter and spirit of section 33, in so far as its policy has been announced with respect to Korea. The intention of the government is that if any other service should be required of this special force, which of course is not being created solely because of the Korean incident, if any police action, for instance, that has a warlike character should be required of it, elsewhere than Korea, the government of course would have to make its decision, but it would immediately call parliament, make that decision known and leave it to parliament to approve or disapprove of it. I think that is the only way the Canadian people would feel they were getting the protection they expect from their representatives.
[M*. Knowles.l

I am glad the hon. member for Nanaimo <Mr. Pearkes) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) provided this occasion for making that perfectly clear. The purpose of this bill is to make it possible to put Canadian forces on active service for the implementation of international obligations resulting from the charter of the United Nations, when such obligations have been recognized by us here in parliament as morally requiring fulfilment. It is also to enable us to put Canadian forces on active service for the implementation of obligations arising under the North Atlantic treaty, because they are obligations that have been incurred with the consent of the Canadian people through their representatives here.
That is the situation, and I do not think anyone would venture to suggest that it should be departed from in any manner whatsoever, in letter or in spirit. If it should become necessary, as it may, to enter into more specific undertakings with members of the North Atlantic treaty or members of the United Nations, those more specific obligations might require some variation in the present procedure; but that variation would have to be brought here and approved by this house before any government would be justified in acting in any different manner. It is our intention to ask that this measure be given royal assent, not at the very end of the present sittings of this parliament but at a time which will permit the required formalities to be carried out. It is intended to have the orders in council applicable to this special case tabled before this session adjourns. If anything else should be required at any future time in order to carry out similar commitments, the government of course would have to take the responsibility of making its decision, but would certainly have to place itself in the hands of parliament within the ten-day period for ratification or disapproval of that decision.
I am sure that is the way everyone would wish matters of that kind to be handled by their representatives, and that all parties would wish that to be the relationship between the government and parliament in that regard. Technically the decision has to be made by the executive branch, but it can be made only in such manner as places it within the power of parliament in the short time provided by section 33 to deal with the government that has made the decision, and to continue its confidence in the government which made the decision or prevent its implementation.

speechtext: No, sir; that would be something which has never beeh done. The government announces to parliament what its policy is, and asks parliament for the ways and means to carry it out. If parliament, on the other hand, on any motion of non-confidence, expresses its disapproval of the conduct of the government, of course the government resigns and some other group forms a government to carry out the will of the Canadian people as expressed by their representatives in parliament.

An order in council will be tabled. It may be that that order in council, for the convenience of the operation, will be in broader terms than if it were possible at this time, for instance, to say that the three destroyers that are now in Korean waters will be the only units of the navy to serve there. It may be that it will be found of advantage to bring one or more of those destroyers back and replace them by others. In order to make that possible, and to make such changes as circumstances would dictate, it may be that the terms of the order in council will have to be broader than the enumeration of those immediately intended to serve. The statement I am making to the house is that this government will not go beyond what has been announced without bringing parliament back to deal with its decision.
There was one other matter raised by the member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), and I think that all members of the government are in agreement with him. These provisions of existing statutes which are to apply to the men enlistedi in the special force cannot be applied without special consideration being given to each of them. It is for that reason the legislation provides that it will be done by orders in council, but those orders in council will not be permanent. Those orders in council will not extend beyond the life of the next session of parliament. We have expressed it in that way so as to make it quite clear that at the next session of parliament we shall have to ask parliament to say whether or not what we have put in the orders in council is sufficient, or whether it goes too far. Whatever we shall have put in

Canadian Forces Act
the orders in council will only apply provisionally until parliament has had an opportunity of dealing specifically with each detail expressed in the regulations.
We felt it would not be prudent, in the short time we had available, to attempt to bring in a complete code of the parts which would apply, and of the manner in which they would apply. We believed we would have to make that code by orders in council, so that if any individual who had enlisted happened to require its application in the meantime it would be available, but that it would not operate as law beyond the life of the next session of parliament. At the next session there will have to be legislation and every line of the regulations will be subject to the approval or disapproval of parliament. I feel confident that we shall maintain, without any impairment whatever, the traditional doctrine of the responsibility of parliament to the people of Canada in respect of all these matters.

I was under the impression that, when parliament was called for the particular purpose of approving the action of the government, there was some operative motion or some other provision which dealt with that particular subject. It seems to me that the point raised by the member for Nanaimo is whether there is in fact any operative resolution before us, or anything in this act which disposes of that question.
