subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
My understanding of the constitutional position is that there is no specific action required by parliament in the form of an affirmative decision. The decision has to be made by the executive branch of the government. It has to be announced and parliament, within the period provided by section 33, has to be put in a position where it can prevent the implementation of that decision by dealing as it may see fit with the government that made it. This act does not in any way derogate from section 33. It does not interfere at all with the application of section 33. It merely provides that the governor in council may place units of the armed forces or components of the armed forces on active service. Whether that be done for service within or outside Canada, when it is done section 33 applies.
Before the end of the last session the government announced to parliament its intention, if naval units were found to be of value, to have them proceed to Korean waters. We announced to parliament that they were already proceeding towards that region from their base on the Pacific coast, and that if any other action of a different character were required parliament would be summoned to deal with the situation. Subsequently a transport squadron was made available to perform duties similar to those that the transport squadrons are constantly performing in our own country or over the Atlantic for the purposes of our service. But when the decision was made that those forms of participation in the action requested by the United Nations should be added to, announcement was made of a decision to raise a special brigade. That could be done without that special brigade being then put on active service. But we felt that it could not be put on active service because of the terms of section 16 of the National Defence Act, and parliament was called. It was announced in parliament that the policy of the government was to raise this force and the required reinforcements and to train them for the purpose of carrying out obligations Canada might have either under the United Nations charter or under the North Atlantic security pact; and also that the intention was, when this land force was ready for front-line action, to have it participate in the Korean action if at that time that was the place where it could be of the greatest utility to the purposes of the United Nations.

We are proceeding in that way and we are still assuming that that is where it could be of the greatest service to the United Nations when it is ready for front-line action; and we have asked parliament to provide us with the ways and means to implement that policy. Should circumstances change, should it be found that that is not the proper thing to do at the time this land force is ready for front-line action, and that something else should be done instead, the government will have to consider that situation; and having made a decision it will have to call parliament, communicate that decision to parliament and put itself in the hands of parliament for approval or disapproval.
I think that is not only the manner in which the terms of section 33 should be complied with but that it is the manner in which traditionally these matters are dealt with by governments and by parliament under our constitutional system. I think it is proper to repeat the assurance that no other line of conduct will be followed by this government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: Owing to the new and very difficult conditions of this warfare, which is not a war, I cannot help feeling that some definition of active service is now required. It is all very well to talk about resisting an act of aggression. We resisted an act of aggression in 1914 when the British Expeditionary Force was sent into the low countries. Certainly a declaration of war had taken place; but there is no declaration of war in Korea. At the same time it is hard to believe that these United States troops who are fighting in Korea are not on active service; and yet our troops apparently are going to be placed on active service and are not going to be at war. It is all so complicated. I suggest that some definition be given of what is meant by being on active service.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: I think the troops there will know that they are on active service.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: Really, that is no answer. It is not what the troops know. The troops may believe that they are on active service. Apparently the Canadian destroyers have been firing shells into the enemy territory. According to press reports, the personnel of the destroyers have been landed and have carried out commando operations. That would be on active service, but they have not been so placed. They would think that they were on active service, but they have not been placed on active service yet. If they are on active service then parliament should have been assembled within ten days. I am not trying to make things difficult. I am asking for what I think is now necessary, namely, a clear definition of what being on active service is.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
The hon. member would not wish me to suggest that perhaps it is not a good thing to have a committee of parliament dealing with the bill, because a committee of parliament dealt with this bill, and he was an honoured and useful member of it, without
Canadian Forces Act
leading to such a definition. But he knows just as I do that the expression has existed from time immemorial in the war act which has so long been one of our texts, incorporated in our laws, in the king's rules and regulations for the forces in Great Britain and Canada, and in every other military text.
It has not been considered desirable so far to define it because it is one of those terms which I think everyone finds difficult to define -so difficult, indeed, that we are here assembled tonight adding a case where we think there is active service and where our troops should go, if it is the intention of the government.
Mind you, I appreciate the hon. member's difficulty, and I must say when I was discussing the bill with my officers we went into this at great length, just as the hon. member has no doubt during his thirty-five or forty years of service. However, in the end we felt we had better leave it as it was.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: But I presume the special brigade, being part of the active component of the army, could also be sent to Korea on service, and they might be fighting pretty hard in Korea and still be termed not to be on active service. It is very complicated.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
We have heard this evening an explanation which, I think, is satisfactory to members in the committee, that men of the navy, the air force and the army will be pretty well looked after. There is another group of men who, as the minister will remember, we felt during the last war should be accepted as a branch of the service. I understand that already four ships of the merchant navy have been chartered to the United Nations for the conveyance of troops, munitions and the like to Korea. What is the position of the government as regards the merchant navy and, in this instance, will they be considered as the fourth branch of the service? I have here a resolution sent to the Minister of Transport. Perhaps I should read it so that there will be a basis on record for my question.
This communication is dated August 23, 1950, and was sent by the national secretary of the Merchant Navy Veterans of Canada to the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, Minister of Transport, and states:
Whereas the government in its advertisements seeking recruits for the army, navy and air force to serve in the Korean conflict promises these men all of the benefits under the veterans charter, and Whereas, four Canadian merchant ships, manned by Canadians, have already been chartered to the United Nations and are already serving in the same war without any of the rehabilitation benefits of the veterans charter, and Whereas, modern warfare with its long-range planes, faster submarines and atomic bombs presents a danger greater than ever before to merchant seamen, be it therefore

Resolved that the government amend the veterans charter to include merchant seamen who will be required to serve in the Korean war and any other war in the future.
We already have a squadron of the Royal Canadian Air Force doing practically the same work as are these men of the merchant navy. I think it is time these men had some understanding as to their status in the present situation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: So far as we know, no members of the Canadian merchant marine are yet directly involved.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: Four ships.

speechtext:
Four ships have been
chartered.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: Chartered, yes. That will become a question for decision by my colleague the Minister of Transport, and for recommendation by him and the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and the committee we propose to set up. There is nothing in this legislation to deal with it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
I may say that this matter
was considered by the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the government during the last session, and I think these men received very shabby treatment. I hope more consideration will be given to their claims this time than was given before.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
I think that consideration
should be given to the suggestion of the hon. member for Royal. Under the acts listed in the schedule to Bill No. 3 there is some provision for a few of the merchant navy men of the last war. Some of them who have pensions have certain rights under these particular acts. I believe there are already four ships with Canadian crews serving in Korean waters. Therefore I think the government would be well advised to consider whether or not there is to be coverage for such men. I hope that the decision will be in favour of giving them the protective benefits of these different acts.
There is one other question that has arisen. I had a letter today from a young man who is thinking of rejoining one of the forces, but he is worried about whether or not the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act will be utilized in full for the protection of men who join the present force. Under section 7 the government need only put a part of the act in effect so far as the men in the new force are concerned. I believe it would be helpful if assurance could be obtained from the government to the effect that the provisions of the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act will apply in full to the men who
Canadian Forces Act
join one of the forces for service in Korea. Of course they want to know that such is the case before they enlist. There is no point in giving up their jobs if they are not going to have protection under this act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
Of course the bill provides
for the governor in council extending the benefits of the act to the classes covered retroactively to the 5th of July this year, at which date ships were sent to Korea. The intention is to look through the many provisions of the act and apply them to just the kind of cases that the hon. member has in mind. That assurance has been given publicly and it will be lived up to. There may be some provisions of the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act which may not be applicable. I am advised that that is so, but the principle and intention of the act will be carried out fully so that men who leave jobs for the purpose of joining the special force will be reinstated in their civil employment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: With regard to the Pension Act, is it the intention that the insurance principle shall apply as from July 5 to all forces which are to be placed on active service?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: Certainly all forces placed on active service for service outside Canada. As to the rest, that remains to be seen.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: I understand from what the minister and the Prime Minister have said that these various veterans acts will be made applicable entirely or in part by regulations and orders in council. I wonder if the minister can give us any indication when the regulations and orders in council will be made public so that men who have enlisted, their families and the general public, may know just what the situation is. I think the general impression that has gone out throughout the country as a result of press releases and so forth is that all the veterans legislation passed following the last war would be applicable to the men of the special service brigade and those in the other services who were on active service. As has *been pointed out by the Prime Minister, some of these things may not be applicable to them. Therefore the sooner the position is made definite the better so far as the government is concerned, the men themselves and the general public. Can we get some idea as to how soon it will be possible to make that information public?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
I quite agree it is very important that it should be done just as soon as possible. The publicity to which the hon. member refers started with the advertisement

Canadian Forces Act
for recruits which appeared, in newspapers on the 7th and 8th of August. It said:
Veterans benefits, reinstatement in civil employment and other appropriate benefits under the veterans charter, as extended by parliament.
It is the intention to put into effect at once measures such as the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act because this may benefit even those who have only been in the force for two or three weeks. Therefore it becomes an absolute necessity that it be brought into effect at once. With respect to some of the other benefits, they are more complicated and more time will be taken to work them out, but so far as the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act is concerned, that must be brought into effect at once, and it will be done.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: Should the Pension Act not be brought into force at once also?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: It will all be retroactive to the 5th of July, but I quite agree that any pension provisions should be brought into effect at once.	.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: Could consideration be given to the application of the veterans legislation to any civilian personnel who are employed in the air transport that may be taking place? We had difficulty in connection with the ferry command personnel in the last war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: That is a question for my colleague, the Minister of Transport. He is here and has heard your suggestion, and it certainly will be considered.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: I am not satisfied with the minister's attitude so far as the merchant service is concerned. We argued that question during the last war and it has been raised many times since the end of the war. I feel that in the last war and during the period since the war the merchant service got a pretty raw deal, and I think the situation should be corrected at this time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: It cannot be dealt with in this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
It can be dealt with in this bill. Section 7 gives the right to the governor in council to amend any of the acts that have to do with rehabilitation, pensions, and so on, as they affect personnel. Changes can be made now lby regulation. If the governor in council so desires he may by regulation -extend the privileges of these acts to anyone who is taking part in this war. I think that should be done for the merchant service. We are not entering into something that is going to be over tomorrow. We are making long-range plans to fight wars in any part of the

world. I do not anticipate fighting a war in Canada. You may have to go to Europe. You certainly have a long supply line now to Korea, and you are not going to get supplies there by plane. The merchant service is definitely going to be a part of wars of the future.
Having in mind the different treatment they received after the last war compared with what was done for service personnel, I think we should do something to correct the situation. The argument was always used that the armed forces were the servants of the state, and that is correct, and that the men in the merchant service were employees of private shipping companies. The private shipping companies exploited them for war purposes but did nothing for them when the war was over. I know boys who lost their legs while in the merchant marine, and who were never fitted with artificial limbs. Today many of them require hospital treatment because of hardships suffered while fighting that war, but they have no redress.
If we anticipate having to use the merchant marine in the next war, instead of being employees of private shipping companies I believe they should be an auxiliary of the naval service, and should go on these boats at naval rates of pay and with some training. Then when the next war is finished they should be treated as the fourth arm of the services. I leave that thought with the minister; I do not think it is good enough to say they cannot come under the act and cannot be considered service personnel, because without a good, efficient merchant service you cannot fight a war in Korea or anywhere else. How are you going to get your supplies there? But the merchant service must get better treatment than they were given during the last war, and I think the answer is to make them a naval auxiliary, and recognize this as the fourth arm of the services. You may not be able to do anything about this now, but the temporary arrangement is that the governor in council may make regulations. I understand that next session the veterans affairs committee will work on a new bill, but in the meantime I want the minister and his advisers to consider the advisability of bringing these men in as I have suggested.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
I can tell the hon. gentleman that while, as he knows and has said, this bill only deals with the Canadian forces, the suggestion he has made has been under consideration by the maritime commission, the

Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence. It is receiving active consideration should another emergency arise.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: I think too much criticism of the treatment given the men of the merchant navy during the last war has been expressed to permit this matter to pass without further consideration. If no provision can be made in this bill then another bill should be brought in containing such provision. There is no reason why the sailors in the merchant ships should have to go without protection, any more than the men in the other services should be left without protection. Since it is after eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I think we had better let this section stand.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: I ask the assistance of the committee to get this bill through tonight. Hon. members have been helpful indeed, and we are now at the last section. I believe hon. members must recognize that the merchant service is not relative to this bill at all, and I have given the assurance that the matter is under consideration. The Senate will be sitting tomorrow, so I ask my hon. friend if we could not possibly get this through tonight.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext:
And I asked the minister something just now, whether another bill will be brought in to look after the men of the merchant navy. In my opinion the convenience of the Senate or of this house is not as important as looking after the welfare of these men. One reason I particularly wanted to have this matter further discussed was that within the last few weeks I took up with the Minister of Transport a case on which I have been working for four or five years. It is the case of a sailor, a young man of wonderful physique, who fell down the hatch of a ship and broke his back. He has no pension, nothing whatever. Thinking I might be able to arrange for him to get some vocational training, I took up the case with the Minister of Transport just a few weeks ago. This young man is six or seven or eleven days short of the required period of service; there are one or two other matters, and just because those little things have not been observed-and it was impossible for him to observe some of them-he cannot even get vocational training. That is the condition that faces every sailor on our ships.
Earlier in the discussion, when the question was raised by the hon. member for Royal, the Minister of National Defence said these men were not yet involved. I understood that though the ships had been chartered they were not yet in service, and that perhaps there was no great urgency in the matter. But now I believe there is urgency, because if
Canadian Forces Act
provision is not made now these men will have no security whatever in case accident or any other mishap shall befall them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
speechtext: I would ask the Prime Minister whether it is intended to make the orders in council placing the forces on active service retroactive to the date on which the act is to be deemed to have come into force.

I would not like to say we could attempt to declare that these men will be deemed to have in fact been on active service since that date. However, that is a matter that will have to be considered by the Department of Justice. [DOT]

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PLACING FORCES ON ACTIVE SERVICE
